#5743. Nanobody Shows Promise in Myasthenia Gravis

— PREVAIL trial found rapid improvement with a once-weekly subcutaneous injection

Results from the phase III PREVAIL trial presented at the American Association of Neuromuscular & Electrodiagnostic Medicine annual meeting showed that treatment with the investigational once-weekly nanobody gefurulimab significantly improved symptoms in adults with anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis, with a safety profile generally comparable to placebo.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, James Winkley, MD, of Baptist Health Medical Group in Lexington, Kentucky, discusses the findings, including the potential convenience of self-administered treatment with the subcutaneous injectable and compatibility with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy.

Following is a transcript of his remarks:

The PREVAIL study was a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with gefurulimab as the treating agent. Gefurulimab is a unique agent in that it's the first nanobody that'll be used in myasthenia gravis, which makes it a smaller molecule, which allows for greater tissue penetration and solubility -- so it can be given as a [subcutaneous] injection rather than the larger monoclonal antibodies, which have to be given in larger volumes underneath the skin or as IV infusion. So this would represent a greater ease of access for patients to have a [subcutaneous], once-a-week injection that doesn't require them to go to the infusion center.

As we had seen in the trial, similar to eculizumab [Bkemv] and ravulizumab [Ultomiris], which are C5 inhibitors, it met its primary outcome of MG-ADL [Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living] reduction, with a minus 4.2 reduction versus 2.1 on placebo, which was statistically significant. We did see a quick onset of action within 1 week, with a statistically significant reduction in the MG-ADL for those patients, as well as 4 weeks for the [Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis].

There were similar side effects between the treatment group and the placebo group, with injection-site reactions being slightly higher in the treatment group, but all of those reactions tended to be mild to moderate. The most common adverse events were headaches, upper respiratory infections, and muscle aches and pains. One thing that was significant at any time we're using complement inhibitors, there were no meningococcal infections. Everybody made sure they were fully vaccinated, and if they'd had to be started prior to 2 weeks, they received antibiotics. But we had a very typical safety profile, as I said, between the placebo arm and the treatment arm -- the side effects were similar.

This is going to make for ease of access for patients. You still have other molecules out on the market. You've got a once-daily complement inhibitor and you've got now a once-every-2-weeks IV infusion versus every 8 weeks. So kind of depending on what the patient prefers, this gives them greater access. We've got an easily portable complement inhibitor that patients no longer are tethered to an infusion center that they have to worry about. When's our next infusion? Do I have access? And I think that's going to be a huge advantage for the patients and their quality of life.

I would say that one thing that's unique about [gefurulimab] is that it is compatible with IVIG. And so the other larger monoclonal antibodies like the FcRn [neonatal Fc receptor] and the larger eculizumab and ravulizumab, it gets recycled by a different mechanism because it goes through the albumin on the FcRn receptor. It was combined with IVIG during the trial, patients could be on stable dosages of it, so it has that advantage of being able to be compared and not have to give supplemental dosing.

So I think that it will have combination with other available medications. I think that's a big advantage for it.

#5740. 2027 Honda CBR1000RR-R Fireblade Has 215 Horsepower And A Titanium Tank

As motorcycle wings get ever bigger and more ostentatious, one bikemaker is bucking the trend. Honda revealed the latest version of its flagship CBR100RR-R literbike at EICMA this year in three trims, two of which lack front wings entirely. That makes it the sleekest looking top-tier sportbike on the market, and it looks to have the performance to match.

Honda says the Fireblade is made up of 75% new parts for 2027, despite making the same 215 horsepower (though the company claims there's more midrange power available than the prior bike). It's sharper looking than the outgoing model, with a more pointed front end and sleeker headlights, and the lower cowl opening has been widened for even further airflow. The coolest upgrades lie beneath all that shiny new plastic: A titanium fuel tank, a bigger air intake, and a chassis that's designed to be 20% less rigid than the outgoing model. Yes, you read that right — Honda made a bike more wobbly in pursuit of speed.

When we think about rigidity in cars, we're talking about preventing the chassis from twisting, something Honda still doesn't want the new Fireblade to do. When a motorcycle is on its side, leaned over through a corner, a bit of flex in the chassis is actually desirable for eating up bumps in the road without upsetting the tires. That's called lateral rigidity as opposed to the torsional rigidity of a chassis twisting, and Honda claims to have lowered the former by 20% on this new bike without affecting the latter. The swingarm has been updated too, losing 12% of its lateral rigidity.

In concert with that new flex, Honda has updated the Showa suspension on the base Fireblade and the electronically-controlled Ohlins on the Fireblade SP. All variants of the bike also get the new titanium fuel tank, though only the SP gets a bit of exposed titanium on the back to probe that's really what the bike's made from. Honda also added a new HRC Works version of the bike, which adds to the SP's pedigree by mounting front aero and removing the electronic suspension in favor of lighter manual components. The company claims the HRC Works bike is a true homologation special for World Superbike, at least when equipped with the warranty-voiding HRC Racing Kit that includes new fuel injection and iginiton systems, as well as a race-oriented shift pattern and updated pivot points.

Of course, given Honda's track record of offering sportbikes in the U.S., it's unclear when exactly the new Fireblade will hit our shores. It's already on European sites as a 2027 model, but our 2027 bike is already confirmed to be a carryover. We'll have to wait, like always, for the latest and greatest. Still, if we can get this bike at the specs Honda's promising, it'll be well worth the wait.

#5739. Another Drug Shows Potential for Functional Cures in Chronic Hepatitis B

— With highest dose of siRNA therapy, 19% achieved a functional cure 24 weeks after treatment ended

Reductions in hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) were observed with a novel small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapy in patients with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, according to a phase II study.

Among patients randomized to monotherapy with one of four doses of the siRNA HRS-5635, all 32 on the highest dose (400 mg) had HBsAg levels less than 100 IU/mL after 48 weeks of treatment, with 88% still at that level 24 weeks after treatment ended.

Among this high-dose group, 16% achieved a functional cure, with an HBsAg clearance level of less than 0.05 IU/mL after 48 weeks -- a percentage that rose to 19% by 24 weeks post-treatment, reported Xieer Liang, PhD, of Southern Medical University in Guangzhou, China, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

"A dose-dependent antiviral response was observed with HRS-5635," Liang said. "All HRS-5635 regimens were generally safe and well-tolerated."

An estimated 240 million people worldwide have chronic HBV infection, including about 640,000 U.S. adults. Chronic HBV can cause liver damage, cirrhosis, liver cancer, and death. Five antivirals and two immune modulators are approved in the U.S. to treat chronic HBV, with treatment regimens lasting from 6 months to over 1 year.

In a previous phase II trial, siRNA therapy with an immunomodulator reduced HBsAg in patients with chronic HBV infection. Last month, the FDA approved another nucleic acid-based therapeutic, the antisense oligonucleotide drug bepirovirsen (Hibsago), for patients with chronic HBV taking antiviral therapy based on results from the B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 studies. In those trials, 19% to 20% of patients with HBsAg levels between 100 and 3,000 IU/mL had a functional cure with bepirovirsen at week 72.

The current trial included patients with chronic HBV on stable nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy who had HBsAg levels over 100 and less than 3,000 IU/mL and HBV DNA levels less than 20 IU/mL. Patients could be hepatitis B envelope antigen (HBeAg) positive or negative, but they couldn't have cirrhosis. All patients received tenofovir amibufenamide during 48 weeks of HRS-5635 treatment.

Mean age ranged from 41.5 to 44.6 years in the four treatment groups, 59.4% to 76.7% were men, and mean HBsAg ranged from 1,058.2 IU/mL to 1,200.4 IU/mL. Most patients were HBeAg negative (65.6% to 73.3%).

The investigators defined functional cure as sustained HBV DNA suppression and HBsAg clearance of less than 0.05 IU/mL, with or without seroconversion, sustained for 24 weeks after treatment.

All four HRS-5635 doses achieved the study's primary endpoint of HBsAg reduction from baseline to week 12, with mean reductions of -1.26 log10 IU/mL in the 50-mg group, -1.90 log10 IU/mL in the 100-mg group, -1.99 log10 IU/mL in the 200-mg group, and -2.12 log10 IU/mL in the 400-mg group.

Among patients in the 400-mg group, 45% converted from HBeAg positive to HBeAg negative after 48 weeks of treatment, a percentage that slid to 27% at 24 weeks after treatment.

In patients receiving the 400-mg dose who were HBeAg negative and had HBsAg below 1,000 IU/mL at baseline, 33% reached the functional cure rate of HBsAg less than 0.05 IU/mL.

Across the four groups, 46.9% to 60% had a treatment-related adverse event. There were only two such events that were grade 3 or higher, and no serious adverse events related to treatment and no deaths occurred. Upper respiratory tract infections were the most common adverse event, occurring in 25% to 33.3% of patients in the four groups.

Alanine transaminase elevations occurred in up to 6.7% of patients during and after treatment, Liang said, but levels were generally stable during treatment, and no elevations reached a grade 3 level.

The follow-up period of 24 weeks after treatment ended was relatively short, Liang cautioned, but a longer-duration extension study is ongoing, along with a phase III trial.

#5738. America's Oldest Active Turnpike Will Pull Down All Its Toll Booths In 2027

Tossing the coins into a metal bin at a toll booth is as dated as looping the dial on a rotary phone. The Pennsylvania Turnpike announced last week that it will switch to open-road tolling at the start of next year. The transition won't be immediate, as contractors have been tasked with removing physical toll booths over the next two years. Officials tout full implementation of open-road tolling as more convenient for drivers and far safer.

Pennsylvania Turnpike opened back in 1940, stretching 160 miles from Harrisburg across the Appalachian Mountains to Pittsburgh. Extensions during the 1950s took the toll road to the state borders with New Jersey and Ohio on either side of the Keystone State, for a total of 360 miles. The turnpike's design served a blueprint for the Interstate Highway System. Besides the payment receptacles, some of the original toll booths are still in place, according to PennLive.

Implementing open-road tolling on the Pennsylvania Turnpike has been a 16-year process. According to the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, officials commissioned a feasibility study in 2010, which deemed the payment system impossible because the turnpike lacked a fiber-optic infrastructure. Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, the toll booths went contact-less in 2020 and relied solely on electronic payments. By 2025, the turnpike began transitioning to open-road tolling.

For those familiar with open-road tolling, overhead gantries photograph the front and rear of your vehicle as you drive past. Antennas are also mounted on the gantries to read EZPass transponders. Sensors embedded in the pavement can determine how many axles your vehicle has, which helps distinguish commercial vehicles. There are no toll plazas, so drivers don't have to slow down and wait for a gate arm. On the Pennsylvania Turnpike, tolls are calculated based on how far you travel along the route, so the gantries monitor when you enter and exit.

There is obviously a massive upfront cost to removing the toll booths and installing the gantries. The improvement work in Western Pennsylvania is estimated to cost $134 million. However, the savings will recoup the costs over time. The transition is expected to save the Pennsylvania Turnpike Authority roughly $25 million a year. For those concerned about the turnpike's history, one of the original 1940 toll booths has already been removed and relocated to the State Museum of Pennsylvania as part of an exhibit on the roadway.

Open-road tolling is also safer than traditional toll plazas. It might seem natural to slow down as you approach the toll booth, but your safety depends on all the drivers behind you doing the same. After investigating a fatal 2024 crash on Interstate 80, the National Transportation Safety Board recommended in September that the Ohio Turnpike "permanently close low-speed tolling lanes and implement fully electronic tolling at its toll plazas." The driver of an SUV abruptly braked and swerved right, attempting to leave the high-speed electronic toll lanes for the booth-controlled low-speed lanes. The SUV cut in front of a tractor-trailer, which struck the smaller vehicle from behind. The crash killed two passengers inside the SUV, as well as seriously injuring a third passenger and the drivers of both vehicles.

Toll booths are gradually going extinct. While I do feel some nostalgia for the ritualistic payment process, open-road tolling is becoming more widespread for good reason. The bridges and tunnels around New York City demolished their toll booths in 2022. Florida's Turnpike and the Illinois Tollway ditched their booths in 2021 and 2024, respectively. Many other toll roads across the country are in the midst of their own open-road tolling transition.

#5735. RFK Jr. Is Ushering in Peptides. As an Oncologist, Here Are My Concerns.

— Clinical evidence hasn't caught up with commercial enthusiasm

On July 13, 2025, at a Las Vegas hotel hosting the Revolution Against Aging and Death Festival, two women were taken away in ambulances. Both had received injections containing experimental peptides at a conference booth. Both became seriously ill and required ventilators. One mixture was believed to contain MOTS-c, P21, BPC-157, and TB4, substances promoted for tissue repair, metabolic health, and longevity.

Both women recovered. Nevada regulators subsequently imposed $35,000 in fines on four parties involved. But investigators could not establish what caused the reactions. They were unable to obtain the injected products for laboratory testing, and their exact contents remain unverified.

That is what bothers me most: two women experienced life-threatening reactions, and investigators could not determine precisely what they received.

Now, Washington is opening a regulatory path for some of these unproven peptides. On October 28, HHS announced an interim enforcement-discretion policy covering six peptides: BPC-157, MOTS-c, TB-500, KPV, Semax, and Epitalon. Under specified conditions, the government does not intend to take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies and physicians compounding these substances while the FDA considers formal rulemaking.

This is not an FDA approval, and it does not establish safety or effectiveness. While the HHS policy includes safeguards that represent progress, the policy also permits wider access before clinical evidence has caught up with commercial enthusiasm.

The question is not whether peptides have therapeutic potential. Many of them do. The question is whether that potential justifies their use before we know whether they work and are safe. The policy followed a July meeting of the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee, which voted eight to six with one abstention, to recommend BPC-157 for the compounding list. It also endorsed five of the other six substances considered.

FDA reviewers had reached a different conclusion. Their briefing documents found insufficient evidence to support adding any of the seven substances. For BPC-157, evaluated for ulcerative colitis, they could not establish effectiveness. For several others, including TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, and Epitalon, human safety studies were absent or extremely limited. Reviewers also identified problems with product characterization.

I have spent much of my career conducting oncology trials, including studies contributing to immunotherapies and targeted agents that are now used worldwide. I have seen promising mechanisms fail to translate into patient benefit and unexpected toxicities emerge after treatments entered routine practice. Clinical development is slow, expensive, and often disappointing. But it is how we distinguish a promising hypothesis from a useful medicine. We should make the review process more efficient, not bypass it.

I see a particular oncologic concern with the premature movement on peptides. Experimental studies suggest BPC-157 may stimulate angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, through pathways involving VEGFR2 and endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Angiogenesis supports normal tissue repair. It is also a process many tumors exploit to sustain growth. This does not mean BPC-157 causes cancer or promotes tumor progression -- we lack human evidence to make that claim. But neither can we definitively exclude such effects, particularly with prolonged exposure or in patients with existing or previously treated malignancies.

In oncology, we routinely encounter treatments acting on pathways shared by normal and malignant tissues. Biological activity beneficial in one setting may have unintended consequences in another. The response should not be to assume harm, but to investigate it.

There is also an indication mismatch. The FDA evaluated BPC-157 for ulcerative colitis, while much commercial interest concerns tendon injuries, exercise recovery, and anti-aging. Evidence for one indication cannot establish safety or effectiveness for another, particularly when doses, routes, and duration differ.

The HHS policy includes safeguards worth acknowledging: appropriately sourced ingredients, documentation of identity and purity, single-ingredient preparations, labeling, serious adverse-event reporting, and patient-specific prescriptions. These address genuine problems in the existing peptide market. Patients already obtain experimental substances through poorly regulated online suppliers. Licensed compounding under defined conditions could reduce some risks.

But we must distinguish between three questions:

Manufacturing controls help answer the first one. Toxicology and clinical studies address the second. Well-designed trials establish the third. A certificate of analysis cannot demonstrate effectiveness. A prescription does not establish a favorable benefit-risk ratio. Adverse-event reporting cannot replace prospective safety studies.

Compounding serves an important clinical purpose, meeting individual needs when commercial formulations are unsuitable. But it should not replace drug development. When experimental peptides are marketed through wellness clinics, telehealth, and social media to thousands of patients for similar purposes, they begin to resemble commercial drugs, even when prescriptions are individualized.

The same principle applies to longevity medicine. Research into cellular senescence, mTOR signaling, metabolic regulation, and cellular reprogramming offers genuine opportunities. I welcome it. But results in mice do not establish human benefit, and widespread use without systematic study does not necessarily generate reliable knowledge. We should accelerate research, not replace it with uncontrolled experimentation.

The HHS policy remains interim, with public comments invited through November 13. That process should address dosing, clinical benefit, long-term safety, adverse-event surveillance, and opportunities to link expanded access to systematic evidence generation.

The choice is not between innovation and regulation. Good regulation enables innovation while protecting patients from uncertain benefits and risks. We have learned this repeatedly in cancer drug development: a compelling mechanism begins a research program. It does not prove a drug is effective.

Innovation deserves encouragement. And patients deserve evidence.

Proposed Rule Would Shut the Public Out and Allow the Administration to Make Sweeping Decisions About 250 Million Acres of Western Public Lands Behind Closed Doors

Yesterday, the Administration announced a proposed Bureau of Land Management (BLM) rulemaking that would drastically weaken the public’s involvement in land use planning and gut protections for Areas of Critical Environmental Concern (ACECs), one of BLM’s primary conservation designations, across 245 million acres of Western public lands. The rule proposes to stifle the voices of local communities by significantly shortening public comment periods and cutting out robust environmental analysis. These changes would make it easier for the BLM to fast-track the sale, transfer, or use of public lands for oil and gas drilling, mining, data centers, and other industrial or commercial development, all while shutting out the American people. The public lands overseen by the BLM contain crucial wildlife corridors, critical habitat, cultural resources and landscapes, watersheds, historic sites, and access to nature and scenery.  The rule threatens to strip vital safeguards for ACECs and environmental review that protect these values, leaving the West’s most sensitive lands vulnerable to irreparable harm.

This aggressive regulatory rollback is the latest chapter in a coordinated, systematic dismantling of America’s public lands. It directly connects to a broader pattern of hostility toward balanced stewardship, which includes the recent rescission of the landmark Public Lands Rule, stated intention to roll back the Roadless Rule and Wilderness policies, the evisceration of National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) standards, and repeated attempts to give away public lands to corporations and developers. This rulemaking contributes to this administration’s singular focus: fast-tracking industrial exploitation and drilling at the expense of our shared heritage, tribal sovereignty and the outdoor recreation economies that sustain rural Western communities.

The proposal comes as Congress debates permitting legislation that would also weaken public participation in decisions affecting shared lands and give more power to development interests.

Planning serves as the foundational blueprints governing public lands for decades; eroding these processes is a profound threat to the long-term health of the West. Making robust environmental review optional and weakening ACEC standards intentionally ties the agency’s hands, preventing it from effectively responding to the compounding threats of climate change, drought, and habitat fragmentation. This action rejects the unmistakable demand from the American public, including local leaders, Tribal representatives, and local elected officials, who have consistently called for public lands to be managed transparently and protected for future generations.

“The Trump Administration is once again plotting to undermine our world-renowned system of shared lands and the public processes that guide their management,” said Jackie Feinberg, Sierra Club’s National Lands Conservation Manager. “Weakening protections and public participation would fast-track the industrialization and privatization of places essential for wildlife, clean water, cultural and historic preservation, and access to nature. We stand firmly against these attempts to cut out the “public” from public lands for the benefit of corporate polluters and profiteers.”

“Gutting transparency, review, and public engagement requirements within the West’s most ecologically sensitive wildlife corridors, watersheds, and cultural resources are the actions of cowards trying to fast-track industrial development at any and all social costs,” said Kara Matsumoto, senior policy director at the Conservation Lands Foundation. “Resource management plans are the blueprints for keeping public lands and waters healthy, and weakening them will weaken local economies and fragile ecosystems. We’ll continue to fight this corporate greed because the overwhelming majority of Americans want more nature protected, not less.”

“The opportunity to review and comment on land management actions keeps the public in public lands.” said Hilary Eisen, federal policy director at Wild Montana. “Resource management plans provide the long-term framework for how vast swaths of public land across the West are managed and it is essential that these plans be crafted with robust public engagement. This proposed rule sidelines the public, as well as local, state, and tribal governments, in BLM land use planning.”

“Resource management planning is meant to provide the public a real say in how BLM manages our shared public lands, and Areas of Critical Environmental Concern are how the agency turns that input into on-the-ground protections for special places and important wildlife habitat,” said Maddy Munson, senior policy and planning specialist at Defenders of Wildlife. “Cutting back public participation and narrowing the agency’s analysis isn’t streamlining, but rather stacking the deck against the places and species that need protection the most.”

“For Nevadans public land is our way of life. Whether we have jobs dependent on mining, grazing, the outdoor industry or just love taking our families camping, these public lands in Nevada are a huge part of who we are. We want to have an active role in determining how these lands are managed and efforts to take the public out of this planning process and weaken protections are just wrong,” said Shaaron Netherton, Executive Director at Friends of Nevada WIlderness. “We need to stand up and keep the public in our public lands.”

“The Trump administration continues to eliminate tools that the Bureau of Land Management has relied on for decades for conserving wildlife habitat, protecting clean water, and working with local communities. The objective is clear: replace the multiple uses and values of our public lands with the singular use of fossil fuel development. That agenda has no footing in Colorado, where 96% percent of Coloradans support conserving public lands and open space and 81% believe oil and gas development is not an acceptable use of public lands,” said Juli Slivka, Senior Director of Policy and Programs at Wilderness Workshop.

“These are the plans that decide whether a valley gets drilled or a trout stream gets protected, and this proposal is built to make those decisions faster and with fewer people in the room,” said Bobby McEnaney, Senior Lands Analyst at NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council). “Cutting the public’s time to weigh in by two thirds, scrapping the full environmental review, and letting a political appointee invoke an emergency to skip the rest is not modernization. It is a way to lock in drilling and mining decisions before anyone can object. Governors get 30 days and no appeal, Tribal plans drop out of the review entirely, and the agency gives itself the power to shrink or erase existing protected areas. Interior should withdraw this proposal and keep the public’s seat at the table.”

“These lands are called “public lands” for a reason: They are owned by the people of the United States. The Bureau of Land Management’s job is to manage them in the public’s interest, for the common good. By so severely restricting opportunities for the public—including, importantly, Tribal Nations—to be involved in planning for their management, the BLM is depriving all of us of our rights as the owners,” said Michael Painter, Coordinator, Californians for Western Wilderness.

“The Trump administration continues its relentless agenda of handing over public lands to corporations,” said Thomas Delehanty, senior attorney with Earthjustice’s Rocky Mountain Office. “Cutting the public out of land management benefits no one except the extractive industries hellbent on controlling these shared resources for their own private gain. Anyone who values public lands must be loud and clear: these attacks end now.”

“Public lands belong to all Americans, and decisions about their future should be made through transparent processes informed by science, meaningful public participation and consultation with Tribes and others in the community. This proposed rule would give us less of a say in the management of 245 million acres of our shared lands and weaken areas of critical environmental concern, the BLM’s primary tool for protecting important natural and cultural sites. It is another clear attempt to give drilling, mining and other development interests more influence over our public lands, in the same spirit as rescission of the BLM Public Lands Rule—and only days after voters delivered a stinging rebuke to this administration’s agenda of doing favors for oil and gas companies and other powerful corporations. Our public lands deserve better, and so do future generations that will inherit them.” said Michael Carroll, BLM Campaign Director, The Wilderness Society.

“In New Mexico, the BLM planning process gives communities, Pueblos, Tribes, acequias, recreationalists, conservation organizations, ranchers, hunters and anglers a real say in what happens to the 13.5 million acres of public land that the agency manages here,” said Sally Paez, senior staff attorney for New Mexico Wild. “Places like the Greater Chaco landscape, the Permian Basin’s remaining wildlife habitat, and our desert grasslands have protections today because New Mexicans showed up and spoke out during planning. New Mexicans shouldn’t be shut out of decisions about their own public lands.”

“In Oregon, the BLM manages 2.6 million acres of Oregon and California Lands that are home to imperiled wildlife, endemic botanical resources, wild rivers, and climate change-mitigating ancient forests that provide outstanding recreational opportunities and socioeconomic benefits to Oregonians and all Americans,” said Susan Jane Brown, attorney with Silvix Resources. “The public and other stakeholders must have a central role in the science-informed stewardship of these cherished resources, all of which will be placed at risk of existential loss with BLM’s proposed rulemaking.”

“Oregon’s high desert community has modeled a long, successful history of federal planners, tribal interests, ranchers, hunters and anglers, recreationists, and conservationists working together to craft management strategies that balance land use and promote conservation across 12 million acres of our shared public lands,” said Mark Salvo, Senior Conservation Advisor for Oregon Natural Desert Association. “Now the Trump administration is recklessly dismissing these decades of collaboration and compromise, trampling public processes, and sidelining those who have worked to protect these lands and resources for future generations–all to advance a narrow agenda of exploitation at the expense of the public interest.”

“The public lands are the people’s lands and the American people have spoken loud and clear. The Bureau’s proposal to cut public participation, reduce protections for cultural sites and critically important habitat, and shortcut environmental analysis is just one more indication that the Trump Administration isn’t listening and will do anything to silence the public, Tribes, and scientists and ignore the reality of what’s happening on the ground,” said Josh Osher, public policy director for Western Watersheds Project. “Millions of acres of climate-stressed Bureau-managed lands are already being degraded by extractive industries, and we need planning rules that include thorough and honest science-based assessments and as many voices as possible to help improve ecological conditions and resilience.”

This is just the latest attempt from the Trump Administration to dismantle our public lands piece by piece,” said Sandra Schubert, Executive Director of Tuleyome. “The proposed Planning Rule undermines protections that ensure that our public lands and wild forests remain accessible and are used sustainably. Resource management plans are built on science and centuries of management experience. They give local land managers and communities the ability to maintain healthy ecosystems while supporting the diverse ways communities depend on public lands. Undermining planning undermines our public lands”

“Once again, Doug Burgum is doing everything in his power to cut the public out of public lands,” said Aaron Weiss, executive director of the Center for Western Priorities. “This new rule gives political appointees in DC more power to shrink protected places and ignore local voices. Public lands belong to all of us, and good land use planning means giving everyone the chance to weigh in.”

“America’s national parks are supported by the public lands that surround them, and this proposal is another blatant attempt to unravel decades of conservation progress that the public overwhelmingly supports,” said Beau Kiklis, associate director of energy and landscape conservation at the National Parks Conservation Association. “Roughly 80 national park sites share a border with BLM lands, and Areas of Critical Environmental Concern have helped protect Dinosaur National Monument from impacts of oil and gas development, support Joshua Tree’s wildlife by protecting the neighboring Pinto Mountains, and protect ancestral sites near Hovenweep among countless others. This is another attempt to sell off and sell out our public lands, and the public deserves a real say before more is lost.”

#5733. Australia's Cheapest New Car Is This $13,000 MG Hatchback, And It's Far From A Stripper

Chinese cars have been beating down on long established performance and luxury car brands for a while now, all while costing a fraction of the price. From jumping over potholes to setting top speed records to beating Land Cruisers in off-road tests and even having emergency water travel capabilities, there are some mighty impressive pieces of kit across the Chinese car industry. What I'm most interested in, though, are the ultra-cheap economy cars that sell for the price of a used shitbox, and that's exactly what the MG3 offers to Australian car buyers. It's a compact hatchback with the face of a plecostomus, which isn't especially exciting, but its $13,020 USD price sure is.

It's no stripper, either. That bargain price includes features like Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, steering wheel controls, air conditioning, a digital driver's display, an auto-hold function, automatic power window switches, and adaptive cruise control with lane centering. It even has a standard feature that the new Toyota RAV4 doesn't even offer on its most expensive trim level that happens to be four times the price of the MG3: padded front and rear armrests. OK, so the MG3's actual MSRP in Australia is $13,890.85 USD at current exchange rates, but the fact that a dealer was even willing to discount it further is remarkable, too.

As you can see from CarSauce's review, the MG3 is woefully slow. Its 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine sends just 109 horsepower and 105 pound-feet of torque to the front wheels via a continuously variable transmission, which results in a leisurely 0-to-62 mph time of 12.57 seconds. It ain't quick, but it gets the job done, and again, it's a $13,000 car. The last car sold in the United States that was near the $13,000 mark was the diminutive Chevrolet Spark, which ran the 0-to-60 sprint in 10.8 seconds in Car and Driver's testing, so the MG3 isn't too far off that pace. Plus, looking beyond straight-line speed (or lack thereof), the reviewer even says it rides great and handles respectably, which are not always the case with bargain-basement cars.

Sadly the MG3's weak engine doesn't equate to exceptional fuel efficiency, with the presenter's real-world economy equating to about 36 mpg on the highway and more like 26 mpg around town. Those aren't abysmal numbers, just perhaps not as good as one might hope from such a weak engine in a tiny car.

Beyond the lower-than-low base price, the MG3's value proposition really comes into focus when you take into account its 10-year manufacturer warranty. For those who say, "why spend $13,000 on the cheapest new car available when you can buy a bigger, better used car for the same price?" Consider the idea of spending $13,000 on a car with a 10-year-long warranty versus spending that same amount on a used car with no warranty. The new car comes with an entire decade of mechanical coverage so the buyer doesn't have to worry about unexpected repair costs for those 10 years, whereas the used car could end up requiring costly repairs within the first year of ownership.

There are some quality concerns noted in the video, including infotainment software glitches and some apparent inconsistencies in the operation of those fancy automatic windows, but considering the price and that stellar warranty, I'd say the pros outweigh the cons in this case. For those who view their cars as another appliance, or those who simply want the financial security of not worrying about repair costs for a whole decade, the MG3 must be a pretty tempting option. Provided you live in Australia, of course — or Mexico, Europe, the Middle East, or other parts of the world where it's pretty damn cheap, too.

#5732. Tesla 'Full Self-Driving' One Step Closer To Recreating Human Driving By Overtaking Bicycles, Exceeding Speed Limits And Misidentifying Road Signs

Humans are imperfect, so at least in theory, robotaxis are supposed to save us by doing all the perfect driving we aren't able to do. Of course, had we poured every dollar that's been spent on robotaxi development into improving public transportation, self-driving cars would feel unnecessary. But the bigger problem is, after all those billions of dollars and years of development, Momentum Mag reports that a recent test of Tesla's so-called "Full Self-Driving" software found that it loved to speed through neighborhoods, illegally pass cyclists, and break other traffic laws. So basically, it drives like your least-favorite neighbor.

Woke 3 already killed the Cybertruck, so Tesla's school bus-passing software could be next on the chopping block after liberals figure out how to make every man a little shorter every time he disappoints a woman. Until then, it's important to know how good or bad the software controlling some of the most popular new cars actually is, which is why Belgian mobility organization johanna.be put the software to the test and found it frequently breaks speed limit laws in areas where drivers are most likely to hit pedestrians or cyclists. So that's not great.

Additionally, while there aren't many places in the U.S. where drivers can't legally pass a cyclist, that isn't the case in Belgium. You'd think fine-tuning the software to account for changes in laws between countries would have been a pretty basic part of Tesla's development, but nope. In johanna.be's testing, it found that Tesla's FSD system "repeatedly tries to overtake cyclists in cycle streets, something that is explicitly illegal in Belgium."

Coincidentally, right around the time johanna.be published the results of its Tesla safety test, the European Transport Safety Council shared the results of a separate safety test. The ETSC found that Tesla's "speed offset" and "contextual max speed" features don't follow United Nations or European Union rules regarding safety, and it's called on member states to reject both features later this year when the EU plans to hold an important vote on advanced driver assistance system regulation.

The ECF is also asking the EU to create a European Road Safety Agency that would act as "an independent EU body able to investigate issues involving automated systems and share the subsequent findings with other Member States." Even before the ETSC got involved, johanna.be's findings were concerning enough to warrant some serious attention from international regulators that Elon Musk wasn't able to gut. As the ECF put it, Tesla's so-called "Full Self-Driving" software (emphasis is the ECF's):

If a human loved to drive at 150% of the posted speed limit, regularly told people the speed limit was higher than it was, and kept trying to make illegal passes, we'd take their license and tell them to take the bus. With robotaxis and cars with driver-assist systems, it should be the same. Until they can prove they actually follow the rules of the road, there's no reason to let them on our roads. We also shouldn't allow automakers to sell driver-assistance systems that haven't been proven safe, either. Even if you disagree, I don't think you need a PhD in traffic safety to understand the argument there.

That said, it's entirely possible that safety researchers are criticizing Tesla for mistakes that every automaker's software makes. The problem with that argument is that johanna.be ran the same test with a Citroën C3 that managed to correctly identify all seven speed limit signs. For comparison, the Tesla got six of the seven speed limits wrong. It only got one correct. Imagine not only being wrong, but being more wrong than the French. Self-immolation is probably the only option.

While we wait to see how the EU's member states vote, the ECF also noted that otherwise docile behavior is no excuse for Tesla's software behaving badly in other ways. As it noted:

the study also found that FSD behaved cautiously and courteously around pedestrians and cyclists in general, yielding early, giving space, and even slowing for a sleepy cat in the road! However, this should not compensate for a pattern of speeding and illegal overtaking in streets that are primarily designed for safe walking and cycling

#5731. Cutaneous Sarcoidosis Could Soon Get an Effective Therapy

— Drug already approved for dermatomyositis passes phase II test

ORLANDO -- Patients with cutaneous sarcoidosis -- a condition with no very effective therapy -- saw dramatic improvement with the dual-acting TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor brepocitinib (Lisraya) in a small phase II trial.

Patients treated with either of two doses of brepocitinib achieved 22-point reductions in Cutaneous Sarcoidosis Activity and Morphology Instrument-Activity (CSAMI-A) scores after 16 weeks, well above the 5-point threshold for clinical relevance, compared with no decrease at all with placebo, reported Misha Rosenbach, MD, of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, and colleagues.

The drug also showed strong efficacy for secondary outcomes, the group found, and no serious adverse effects were recorded. The study was published in JAMA Dermatology and was also presented here at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting.

Cutaneous sarcoidosis might be the biggest treatment challenge in all of dermatology. Corticosteroids have long been the mainstay of therapy, but are only sporadically effective and, among patients who do respond, relapses are common. Second-line treatments such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, or tetracyclines don't do much better. Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors were recommended as third-line therapy in a 2021 treatment guideline, but on very poor evidence. A French case series published in 2017 suggested TNF inhibitors could be used effectively, but the authors noted that adverse effects and discontinuations were common, and one-third of patients relapsed while on therapy.

With this dismal treatment landscape in mind, clinicians have turned to Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors as a possible alternative. Drugs such as tofacitinib (Xeljanz) and upadacitinib (Rinvoq) have been tried with some success, but only in single case reports and small series. Good results were also reported last year with the currently approved TYK2 inhibitor deucravacitinib (Sotyktu) in one patient.

All that bodes well for brepocitinib, which the FDA approved in August for dermatomyositis, and the phase II data in sarcoidosis appear to bear out the promise. Rosenbach and colleagues enrolled 31 patients, randomizing them in a 3:2:2 ratio to 45 or 15 mg/day of brepocitinib or placebo; they could stay on their conventional non-targeted therapies, but oral steroids were withdrawn over the first 8 weeks and topical steroids were stopped at randomization.

Patients were generally in their 40s and 50s. Mean disease duration varied in the three arms: about 10 years for the placebo and high-dose brepocitinib groups, and 4 years in the low-dose group. CSAMI-A scores averaged about 34 at baseline. Roughly 40% of participants had lupus pernio, the lumpy discolored facial and cranial lesions that may be the worst symptom of cutaneous sarcoidosis. Pulmonary sarcoidosis was also common in the sample.

Change from baseline in CSAMI-A score was the primary outcome measure. While no difference between the two brepocitinib doses was seen for this endpoint, "high-bar" outcomes showed some gaps. All patients in the high-dose group saw at least 10-point reductions in CSAMI-A scores, compared with 73% on the low dose (and 14% in the placebo group). Similarly, "functional remission," defined as a score below 5, was achieved by 62% with 45 mg versus 46% on 15 mg, and none receiving placebo.

Perhaps most encouragingly, all five patients in the 45-mg group with lupus pernio achieved 10-point reductions in CSAMI-A scores. Patients on the active drug also had substantial improvement in skin-related quality of life, whereas the placebo group actually had deterioration. (The near-total lack of improvement with placebo for any efficacy outcome testifies to just how difficult cutaneous sarcoidosis is to treat.)

With regard to safety, one patient in each arm quit therapy because of adverse events. But none were rated as serious. One patient on 45 mg showed a creatinine kinase elevation, and one developed anemia. Otherwise, no "special interest" events were seen; these included cardiovascular events, viral reactivation, transaminase elevations, venous thromboembolism, and malignancies.

Following his conference presentation, Rosenbach was asked where brepocitinib might fit in the treatment algorithm for cutaneous sarcoidosis. He cautioned that it was still early to speculate on that, since a larger phase III trial is only just getting underway. But if those data are like those he reported, "I imagine many patients would get it as first line," he said.

He was also asked about effects on pulmonary and joint manifestations, which are common in cutaneous sarcoidosis. He said the studies thus far have really focused on skin, and he couldn't say much about other symptoms. He added, though, that these would almost certainly be examined in the phase III trial.

Brepocitinib's developer, Priovant Therapeutics, expects primary results from the phase III study at the end of 2028. Rosenbach said the 45-mg dose will be the one tested for potential approval. Additional trials are underway in uveitis and lichen planopilaris; there's no indication, however, that Priovant plans to challenge deucravacitinib, which is approved for plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis.

#5729. Polestar Formula 2030 Concept Makes Us Hope Polestar Will Be Back In America By 2030

Chinese-owned Polestar was banned from selling cars in the U.S. back in June, and like a scorned ex showing you what you're missing after a breakup, it's now revealed one of the coolest designs in recent memory: the Formula 2030 concept car. Look at what they took from us.

It's got a low, wide, shooting brake shape. The big front door, little rear door setup is pure enthusiast bait, and the switchgear inside looks like it came straight off of professional audio equipment. The Formula 2030 isn't just a for-show concept car, either, because Polestar says it will indeed "point towards future design direction for the brand."

Specifically, "various design attributes" seen here will actually show up in the next-gen Polestar 2 and upcoming Polestar 7 compact SUV. The Formula 2030 is billed as a compact four-door sports car, not really fitting neatly into any existing segment. It sits lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, fits between the 2 compact sedan and 7 size-wise, and is probably closest to the Polestar 4 in spirit.

It already looks great at a glance, but things get way more interesting once you start opening stuff up. Both the hood and rear hatch open up clamshell-style, exposing the natural fiber composite chassis underneath and orange Öhlins dampers. The half-size rear doors are coach doors, giving the Formula no B-pillar and a huge opening when all doors are open.

Inside, a very curved instrument screen measuring 20 inches sits on top of the steering column while a 12.2-inch center touchscreen sits in the middle. That touchscreen can physically lower when the driver switches drive modes to Performance, and raise when the car is in Autonomous. Below this screen is an array of up to eight customizable rocker switches and knobs. You can swap the specific switches or knobs out, like you can with, say, a pro-grade video game controller, and their individual functions can also be configured to your liking. All four bucket seats sit low in the cabin and get inflatable bolsters and cushions for better support.

I've never really thought about how rare four-spoke wheels are, but looking at the 22s on this Polestar concept, I'm simultaneously sad that they aren't more common but also completely understand why that's the case. They're definitely weird, but I also sort of dig it?

It all adds up to a funky yet beautiful design that makes us hope Polestar will return to the U.S. market by the Formula 2030's namesake. Given the political conditions that led to its banning and how those tides are turning in this country, that scenario actually feels like a real possibility.

#5727. Michèle Mouton Driving A Quattro S1 Up Pikes Peak Is The Coolest Way To Promote Audi's New Q7

The first thing that comes to mind when you mention Quattro is probably Audi's 1980 Group B rally car. It makes perfect sense that the German manufacturer would lean on that legacy when promoting its new Q7 and SQ7 SUVs that have the trademarked all-wheel-drive system, but the company did something much cooler for its new ad campaign: Audi reunited Michèle Mouton with a Quattro S1 at the iconic Pikes Peak hill climb. The 1982 World Rally Championship runner-up still looked at home behind the wheel of the 493-horsepower rally monster.

Audi's new ad campaign titled "Performance Runs in the Family" features a pair of videos: a typical 30-second TV spot, and a 4-minute short with Mouton driving a Quattro S1 up Pikes Peak. During the visually stunning drive up the Colorado mountain, she reminisced about the animosity she faced during the 1985 hill climb, her winning run, and how the ascent has changed in the 41 years since.

Mouton was the first woman and the first non-American to win the Pikes Peak International Hill Climb. The Frenchwoman set a record time of 11:25.390 up the treacherous 12.4-mile ascent, besting the previous record set by Al Unser Jr. in 1983 by 13 seconds. Mouton is still effortlessly cool, still delivering pointed one-liners as naturally as the rest of us breathe. During the revival run, she noted, "When I was at this spot in the race, I had no time for feelings."

The 30-second TV spot mixes archival footage of Mouton during the Group B era with footage of a 2027 Audi SQ7 driving up Pikes Peak. To emphasize the campaign's legacy theme, the ad features Mouton alongside her daughter, Jessica. The third-generation Q7 isn't as nimble on the twisting mountain roads as a Group B rally car, but that isn't the point. The SUV's new styling looks just as aggressive and far more comfortable for a family. Vito Paladino, Audi of America's President, stated in a release:

"Audi's story of quattro didn't end with rally racing. That connection between performance and everyday capability is what makes quattro such a defining part of our brand. The all-new Audi Q7 family carries that legacy forward, bringing together Audi's performance heritage with the innovation and engineering that define the next generation of our vehicles."

The 1985 Pikes Peak International Hill Climb was Mouton's last event with Audi before she departed for her farewell season with Peugeot. The Frenchwoman and her accomplishments will forever be tied to Audi. Mouton's four WRC victories with the Audi Quattro are a legacy every four-wheel-drive model produced by the German automaker inherits. It's not merely laurels to rest on, but a level of performance that Audi has to honor.

#5725. Enfortumab Vedotin-Based Treatment Solidified for Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer

— Experts discuss survival gains and whether all patients need adjuvant therapy

In this exclusive roundtable video from MedPage Today, three expert leaders in the field of bladder cancer discuss the latest emerging data presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) congress.

Moderator Matthew Galsky, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City, is joined by David Aggen, MD, PhD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, and Stephanie Berg, DO, of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

In this first of four episodes, they examine findings from the VOLGA trial, including the survival benefits of enfortumab vedotin (EV; Padcev) plus durvalumab (Imfinzi) and whether all patients need additional treatment following cystectomy.

Following is a transcript of their remarks:

Galsky: Hi everyone. Welcome to MedPage Today ESMO Roundtable on [genitourinary] cancers. And I'm Matt Galsky. I'm a medical oncologist focusing on bladder cancer at the Tisch Cancer Institute at Mount Sinai in New York. And I'm joined today by Dr. David Aggen from Memorial Sloan Kettering and Dr. Stephanie Berg from the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. So welcome both of you. Thanks for joining.

Galsky: Absolutely. We had a pretty consequential set of data from ESMO this year on localized bladder cancer, both muscle-invasive disease and non-muscle-invasive disease. So over the next bit of time, I thought we would talk about some of the more important data, some of the potential practice-changing or practice-informing data, and would love to get your opinion on a set of studies that I think probably are the most important to talk about. And by the end of the discussions, I'm hoping that each of us can identify maybe immediate practice implication related to the data or an unanswered research question that you think should be tackled next.

So I thought we'd start with VOLGA, and I was going to present just a brief overview of the VOLGA study for the audience, and then would love to get your input on VOLGA. So just as a bit of context, we all know that from the KEYNOTE-905 and KEYNOTE-B15 studies in cisplatin-ineligible and cisplatin-eligible patients, respectively, that the regimen of perioperative enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab [Keytruda] with cystectomy is a standard treatment approach for patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

VOLGA tested a variation on this theme. So VOLGA enrolled patients who were cisplatin-ineligible or -declining and patients were randomized to receive either cystectomy alone, as was considered a standard of care at the time, or neoadjuvant treatment with enfortumab vedotin plus durvalumab for three cycles and then adjuvant durvalumab.

So a couple of differentiators from KEYNOTE-905: one, the use of durvalumab rather than pembrolizumab. The second is that in the adjuvant phase of treatment, there was no enfortumab vedotin given, which there was in KEYNOTE-905. In this study, it was only adjuvant immune checkpoint blockade. There was a third arm of the study and that included tremelimumab [Imjudo], a few doses of tremelimumab in the neoadjuvant and then one dose in the adjuvant setting, I believe.

The triplet regimen with tremelimumab demonstrated an improvement in disease-free survival, or event-free survival [EFS] rather, but not an improvement in overall survival [OS] -- yet. But the regimen of enfortumab vedotin plus durvalumab showed an improvement in event-free survival and an improvement in overall survival. The hazard ratios look pretty good, 0.51 for OS, 0.58. I'm sorry, 0.51 for EFS and 0.58 for overall survival. And I didn't really comment on the path CR [pathologic complete response] rates in the study, but would love to get your thoughts on that as well.

So Dr. Aggen, what do you think of this study? What does it add to the treatment of patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer?

Aggen: I think that VOLGA really solidifies that enfortumab vedotin with a checkpoint is the standard for patients with muscle-invasive disease. The two phase III trials now in cisplatin-ineligible patients showing a huge benefit in terms of event-free and overall survival to giving neoadjuvant therapy.

I do think a couple key takeaways are that it's unclear the adjuvant contribution of enfortumab vedotin for some patients, and VOLGA really brings that into question, that some patients may not need enfortumab vedotin for an extended course after surgery. It's really on us to figure out who those patients are. There seems to be comparable EFS with a more limited duration of EV therapy.

The second thing though that's sort of of interest is the pathologic complete response rate in VOLGA, which was about 45% by investigator assessment and then closer to 40% actually when it was centrally reviewed. That is slightly lower than what we saw with all the caveats of cross-trial comparisons in EV-303/KEYNOTE-905 and EV304/KEYNOTE-B15.

And so I do think that's something that we're going to be talking about. A key theme of the meeting though in some of the other trials we may discuss later on is that path CR rate doesn't necessarily equate with long-term outcome. There were path CR rates with pembrolizumab in combination with cisplatin on the order of about 44% reported, and that did not equate to the same EFS and OS benefit.

So for me, the key takeaway is that for a patient with muscle-invasive disease, we should be having a conversation about ADC-IO [antibody-drug conjugate and immuno-oncology] therapy. I think that the onus is on us to figure out how much and who needs additional adjuvant treatment based on which regimen you select.

Galsky: Thank you. Dr. Berg, so Dr. Aggen mentioned that not everyone might need adjuvant EV, maybe not everyone needs adjuvant immune checkpoint blockade. Are there criteria that you use in clinic right now to determine what to do after surgery?

Berg: I think right now I'm still using the trial criteria and offering adjuvant, at least immunotherapy, and EV for those I think that can tolerate it. We all know radical cystectomy is quite tough and if you can try to get it in the window of time, but I completely agree with high-risk disease, it's important. But then if they have path CR or low risk, still T1 with a treatment effect, you really question is adjuvant anything needed, especially adjuvant EV.

And when you think about toxicities, like Dr. Aggen mentioned, especially with peripheral neuropathy, thankfully they were getting less EV in VOLGA, just the three cycles, but that can be really life-changing for patients and it's something that we really have to think about. What are we going to be doing for them if we eliminated micrometastasis and increasing that risk for permanent toxicity? So it's something I think the question isn't completely answered, but I think this data really helped at least bridge a little bit of the gap about having a broader discussion about adjuvant EV, and we're going to hopefully see some trials in this space.

And I just wanted to add that this also made me realize, and to tell our patients, that you can still get neoadjuvant treatment and go to surgery. I think it just confirmed that it's not really leading to more complications and it's really established how we're doing, as Dr. Aggen said, EV and ICI [immune checkpoint inhibitor], because I think we're not saying ICI specific now, and I'm sure once NCCN [National Comprehensive Cancer Network] gets a hold of it, we'll have a different wording for that language.

Galsky: Dr. Aggen, what do you make of the CTLA-4 blockade data? Sort of a checkered history in urothelial cancer so far.

Aggen: Unfortunately, it's been difficult to see a clear long-term benefit with CTLA-4 and bladder cancer like we've seen historically in kidney cancer. And it seems that the additional toxicity doesn't necessarily equate to an improvement in terms of pathologic complete response rates and not yet in terms of overall survival. Probably there's a subgroup of patients with immune-infiltrated tumors maybe that could benefit from CTLA-4, but I just don't think we have a clear sense of who those patients are at the moment.

Galsky: Thank you. So maybe one quick take home from both of you regarding VOLGA. How does this impact your practice Monday morning?

Berg: I can go first. I would say it fits in a sense that I'm going to say without cisplatin eligibility, I'm going to offer EV and ICI for patients prior to radical cystectomy if that's what they're choosing for their perioperative care. And that's what I'm going to go with.

Aggen: I think that if 10 years ago, Matt, we told Dean Bajorin that we'd have hazard ratios of 0.51 in muscle-invasive disease, he would've had a hard time believing us. I think that VOLGA reaffirms that ADC-IO therapy is the backbone of neoadjuvant therapy. And there's going to be, I think, a lot of shared decision making when it comes to adjuvant therapy. Certainly for patients with residual disease at cystectomy, those are patients who in my mind absolutely should continue ADC-IO therapy postoperatively.

Galsky: And I think you make a great point. We have two contemporary studies now with comparisons of systemic therapy with cystectomy versus cystectomy alone. It's pretty unusual to have that in solid tumors in this age where systemic therapy is integrated into clinically-localized disease across the board. So there's really no surgery-alone trials anymore.

So two contemporary studies both showing marked improvement in outcomes with perioperative systemic therapy. I think that really sort of seals the question about whether or not perioperative systemic therapy is needed in muscle-invasive bladder cancer. So thank you for those comments.

#5724. NASA Pushes Further Ahead With The Non-Space Side Of Its Mission, Teases New Experimental Plane

NASA has unveiled, sort of, its newest experimental plane. And by that, the agency appears to mean a plane meant to conduct experiments, rather than the plane itself being the experiment. Called the X-70 Fractal, the aircraft's primary selling point is its modular design, both inside and out. This means that payloads can be swapped out easily, whether they are hanging off the wings or nestled inside the plane. Even the flight controls can be reconfigured in case the agency wants to test different ways for the pilots (and it is piloted) to maneuver. The X-70 is really a platform to allow for a wide array of experiments on a single airframe, rather than creating a bespoke airframe to conduct one mission, like the X-59 is doing now.

As for the plane itself, the X-70 Fractal is... well, more announcement than vehicle, at least for now. NASA says that it can carry 2,000 pounds of science equipment and take off with up to 10,000 pounds total. It will fly up to 45,000 feet in altitude, far above most airliners and well into the stratosphere. It will go up to 1,500 nautical miles, broadly on par with an F-35. It also looks like an F-35, I think, maybe? For images, all we've got is this misty photo that looks AI generated. NASA seems to want to copy the energy of the F-47 and F/A-XX reveals, which are also foggy renderings and not actual photographs. Show me you're making an airplane without showing me you're making an airplane, I guess.

NASA achieves such historic feats in space that it's easy to forget that it is also an "Aeronautics" administration. Part of its remit is to push forward the boundaries of aviation here on this planet, which NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has renewed focus on. Isaacman himself is a pilot who owns his own MiG-29 Soviet fighter jet, so this is an area of personal interest for him. In fact, he's promising that more experimental aircraft are on their way; rumors abound that the agency may be returning the famous SR-71 Blackbird, the fastest plane ever made, to service.

By doing so, NASA does important R&D on airplane technology that is then released into the public record, to the benefit of all aviation companies and everyone who flies on their products. That's the whole point of the X-59, which is trying to reduce the impact of sonic booms enough to make commercial supersonic planes financially viable. In addition, NASA's latest budget points to aviation as an area of strategic competition, per Wired. To that end, it may do some research alongside the Pentagon as well. This is where something like the X-70 is useful: it could do scientific, commercial, or military research as needed, simply by swapping out equipment payloads via its modular design. Now all NASA needs to do is, you know, build it, possibly with a contractor. Details!

#5723. DOJ Slaps Lyft With $53 Million Lawsuit For Allegedly Discriminating Against Disabled Riders

The U.S. Department of Justice is suing ride-hailing company Lyft, accusing it of routinely discriminating against people with disabilities in direct violation of federal law. The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, alleges that Lyft and its drivers "routinely refuse to serve" people with disabilities, such as folks who use stowable wheelchairs or ride with service animals. The DOJ also accused the San Francisco–based company of imposing cancellation fees on people who were denied service and charging passengers with disabilities higher fees and unnecessary surcharges.

The Justice Department sought $53 million in damages for the "hundreds, and likely thousands" of customers it said Lyft and its drivers had wronged, and it's the latest in a series of legal actions the government has taken against major ride-hailing companies related to alleged Americans with Disabilities Act violations, according to Reuters. Just last year, the DOJ accused Uber of similar behavior and sought $125 million in damages. Uber says it has since committed to expanding access and improving the experience of riders with disabilities.

The department said Lyft failed to change its policies and practices to prevent this sort of discrimination, and it failed to adequately train drivers and customer service representatives about their obligations under federal law, The New York Times reports. On top of the $53 million in damages for passengers, the government is asking the court to consider a civil penalty against Lyft.

Uber, and now Lyft, have disagreed with the allegations vehemently. Here's what Lyft told The Times in a statement:

Discrimination has no place in the Lyft community. We have longstanding policies requiring drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or use foldable mobility devices, and drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation.

It should be noted that Lyft says it is fully cooperating with the Department of Justice through this entire process.

Unfortunately for everyone involved, this is not the first time Lyft has been in hot water over discriminating against folks with disabilities. As The Times points out, the company resolved allegations that its drivers denied services to people who used wheelchairs or walkers in 2020. Admittedly, the scope and penalties were far smaller back then, but it's a big deal nonetheless. Six years ago, it agreed to revise its policies and pay four passengers thousands of dollars in damages, along with a $40,000 civil penalty.

#5722. Science For The People, Right On!

Today United for the Future launches at COP31 today with a plan to unite 100 million people in peaceful, non-partisan marches in cities worldwide. Their goal is to assemble the largest coordinated climate demonstration in history in order to put climate action back at the top of the political agenda.

Backers of the initiative include Christiana Figueres, former UN climate chief and a key architect of the Paris Agreement; Bill McKibben, author and co-founder of 350.org; Ram Ramanathan of Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego; and Sandrine Dixson-Declève, honorary president of the Club of Rome.

Together, they beckon citizens around the world: “Protect our future. Act on the science.” Their call asks governments to stop weakening climate protections and to deliver action that cuts emissions and protects nature in line with science.

Limiting temperature rise to a 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above the preindustrial levels of the early 1800s was a goal established during the 2015 Paris Agreement. Since then, it’s been a focus of international climate negotiations, and one that’s often been politically contentious.

“For too many people, climate change is deadly,” UN climate chief Simon Stiell said at COP31. “At this COP, nations face a choice: electric or shock. Rewire the global economy for the electric age. Or accept ongoing fossil fuel cost pain for families, firms, and governments.”

Global carbon emissions from fossil fuels are projected to decrease by 0.4% in 2026, driven by expansion of solar and wind power and the Iran conflict, according to new research by the Global Carbon Project.

Then there’s the recent blue tsunami that took place in the US midterm elections, which served as a condemnation of the Trump administration. Historian and activist Rebecca Solnit exclaims, “It was a dam breaking, the dam that held back the will of the people, the people of the world’s most diverse country, the people who believed in their own rights and equality and in the rights and equality of others.”

Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) admonishes the new Democratic majority to deliver on its campaign jargon. “No more empty rhetoric. No more telling us how terrible Trump and the Republicans are. No more excuses,” he says. “We now have the votes to pass legislation that will demonstrably improve the lives of millions of working families. And that’s what we must do.”

Sanders insists that the time is now to “act boldly.” Democrats can create millions of good-paying jobs, he continues, “by moving our energy systems away from fossil fuels to energy efficiency and sustainable energy.”

David Fickling outlines in Bloomberg this week that renewables have already made tremendous headway, to the point that “sometimes, change comes at you so fast that you forget to congratulate yourself on what you’ve achieved.”

In 2025 clean energy sources generated nearly the same amount of electricity as the entire world consumed in 1996. About half of that electricity, Fickling continues, was sourced from wind and solar power.

“Instead of concentrating on squeezing the final tons of carbon from electricity,” he offers, “governments need to make abundant clean power cheap enough to drive fossil fuels out of everything else — in particular, electric cars and trucks, home heating systems, and the sort of low-temperature heat used in food and paper manufacturing.”

In that new cohort of leaders is William Lawrence, co-founder of the climate action movement, Sunrise. The Michigan Democrat flipped a House seat and sees clean energy as a way to fulfill campaign promises.

He describes clean energy tax credits as a good place to start.

“It’s a huge issue not just for the climate, but for our energy security,” he states. Climate is as important to energy security as it’s ever been, he tells Claire Brown of the New York Times.” People are experiencing the rising costs of fuel due to the war and volatility around the world. And we can all see the value of being able to have cheap, clean renewable energy that doesn’t depend on the global commodity markets.”

Stine, the executive director of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology during the Obama administration. “If the policy question is outside their own expertise, they know how to call on the best experts.”

The incoming scientists represent “a real repudiation of what has been two terrible years for science and public health,” Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, chronicles for Alexander Nazaryan of the New York Times.

Where will the US Congress go from here? Rebecca Solnit muses, “What comes after hope, when hope is realized, when hope is no longer necessary?”

Clean energy expert Steve Hanley has an answer to that question. “The guiding star for all policy decisions going forward should be reducing carbon and methane emissions.”

Did you know that electric motors convert 90% of the energy they consume into motion, while an internal combustion engine converts less than 30%? Not everyone is aware of the efficiency of electrifying everything, though. “In almost all circumstances, electrification is a good thing,” says Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister of climate change and energy and COP31’s president of negotiations.

Now we’ll see if Congress can translate political subterfuge into clean energy reality.
