#5720. At $17,000, Is This Meyers Manx SR2 A Super Cool Cat?

Today's Nice Price or No Dice Manx SR2 is the second VW-based kit car offered by legendary builder Bruce Meyers, and it features a design he thought would be far harder to copy than his first: the ubiquitous dune buggy. Let's decide what such a unique bit of car culture should cost.

With the recent discontinuation of the Supra, fans eager to carry the torch of non-tepid Toyotas are left with only the GR86 coupe and the crazily expensive GR Corolla as rides of choice. The fact that Toyota couldn't be bothered to develop the last-generation Supra on its own, leveraging BMW for most of the under-skirt bits, makes it questionable whether the company even has any interest in sporty cars anymore. Instead of pulse-pumping sports cars, the company offers around a dozen five-door crossover-style vehicles, since that's what sells these days.

That wasn't always the case; in addition to the Supra, Toyota once offered a rally-bred version of the stalwart Celica and a full-blown mid-engine sports car in the MR2. We looked at a 1993 Toyota MR2 on Tuesday, a non-turbo car that otherwise had all the options we'd want. Unfortunately, that non-turbo nature and a non-working A/C compressor called into question its $14,000 asking price. In the end, you all gave that a heave-ho in an 85% 'No Dice' downvote.

A lack of taint-tightening Toyotas doesn't mean that the automotive landscape has totally turned into dullsville, however. There are plenty of fun and interesting cars and, yes, even trucks, out there from which to choose when something more than sleepwalking self-driving is in order. But what if you wanted something crazier than what's on the menu right now from the ever-shrinking cadre of entertaining cars on the market? That's when a rare opportunity like today's Meyers Manx SR feels especially apt.

The SR2's creator, Bruce Meyers, grew up living the California dream. A bohemian artist and engineer, Meyers spent his early adult years surfing, off-road racing, and teaching himself to mold fiberglass as a boat builder. His talents all merged in the creation of the original Meyers Manx dune buggy, introduced in 1964.

Built on a VW Type 1 platform shortened by 14.5 inches, the Manx immediately became an icon and set off an industry of copycats. Meyers went to court to stop the copiers from making dime on his design, but to little success. Taking another tack, Meyers' next street kit, the Manx SR2 (Street Roadster), was far more complex, featuring 10 body panels (as opposed to the original Manx's two) and iconic scissor-style doors. Unfortunately, the cost of the lawsuits, along with nasty letters from the IRS, ate away at Meyers' company finances, and he closed the doors in 1971. By that time, fewer than 200 Manx SR body kits had left the Fountain Valley factory.

This is one of those rare SR models, built on a VW Beetle platform, but powered by a Chevy Corvair air-cooled six. Unlike most automotive engines, the Corvair mill spins counterclockwise, so the car also has the Chevy four-speed manual gearbox instead of a VW transmission. According to the ad, the added power (likely around 140 horsepower gross) makes the car "fly!"

The car rolls, appropriately enough, on a set of Western Bullet Torque Thrust-style wheels wrapped in white-letter BF Goodrich tires. They sit proud in the exaggerated wheel arches, looking almost comically large in comparison to the car's miniature 80-inch wheelbase.

Another way Bruce Meyers and co-designer Stewart Reed sought to improve upon the original Manx was through weather protection, fitting the SR2 with an optional fabric targa top and side curtains. This car appears to have neither, nor does it even seem to have a windshield wiper, making it a fair-weather friend. It's also missing one of the front bumperettes, which could be hard to find. Other than those issues, the car's exterior appears to be in really good shape, with the paint still shining and everything else still intact.

Make no mistake, though: this car is a project that needs some work. The seller claims the seats are "ready for upholstery," implying that they have somehow been pre-gaming for the effort. There's also apparently an issue with the scissor doors (a first, by the way), as they seem to be sitting in place in most of the pictures but aren't actually attached by their hinges. That's evident in the interior photo, where the passenger-side door is absent entirely.

The interior itself is in rough but serviceable condition. Those upholstery-ready seats are nothing more than fiberglass shells with an inch or so of ancient foam padding, and they look about as comfortable as sitting on an orange crate. The rest of the cabin is black-painted fiberglass with a bare VW floorpan. Neither element looks too egregious.

The dashboard offers a full complement of VDO gauges with the tach hilariously pegged at a 4,500 rpm redline. The speedometer's odometer inset shows 30,461 miles, but the ad claims an "I don't know" 99,999 as the mileage. On the plus side, the car's title is clean, and the seller claims it is licensed as an "asvr," which I believe means home-built, with a 1987 VIN assignment.

As noted at the outset, this Manx SR is one of those rare birds to catch in the classifieds. It's not crazy rare, though, as there's another with the same Corvair power, but in orange and with a salvage title, offered through one of the classic car classifieds.

This one, despite some questions and missing pieces, looks like a great foundation for a light restoration. That would result in a unique and fun sport-about for weekend and car show duty. Find the top and side curtains, and rain won't be the hindrance the car currently faces.

With all that in mind—and yes, it was a lot—what do you think about this Manx SR? More importantly, how do you feel about spending $17,000 to buy it? Is that a fair price, given the car's rarity and condition? Or does that price make you want to turn tail and run?

#5719. Next-Gen Anticoagulant Lands FDA Nod for Secondary Stroke Prevention

— First-in-class factor XIa inhibitor was supported by the OCEANIC-Stroke trial

The FDA approved asundexian (Sunharbo) as the first factor XIa (FXIa) inhibitor for secondary stroke prevention, the agency announced on Monday.

Asundexian, an oral, direct, small-molecule inhibitor of FXIa, is indicated for use in combination with antiplatelet therapy to reduce the risk of stroke in adults following a recent mild-to-moderate non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or a high-risk transient ischemic attack. Its selective mechanism of action is associated with a lower risk of complications compared with available anticoagulants.

"Stroke is a leading cause of disability and death in the United States, and survivors are at risk of having another stroke," said Hylton Joffe, MD, MMSc, director of the Office of Cardiology, Hematology, Endocrinology, and Nephrology in the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, in the FDA's press release. "Today's approval represents a meaningful advance for patients and healthcare providers seeking a new option for secondary stroke prevention."

The approval was backed by the large phase III OCEANIC-Stroke trial in which treatment with asundexian led to a 26% relative reduction in the incidence of ischemic stroke through 780 days compared with placebo (6.2% vs 8.4%, HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65-0.84).

Importantly, there was no significant increase in major bleeding risk among asundexian recipients who were on a 50-mg once-daily dose (1.9% vs 1.7% with placebo, HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.85-1.44).

Of note, asundexian is not approved for stroke prevention in people with atrial fibrillation (Afib). The FXIa inhibitor failed among Afib patients in the phase III OCEANIC-AF trial, which was stopped early for lack of efficacy.

Asundexian is not to be used concomitantly with combined P-glycoprotein and strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., carbamazepine, rifampin, St. John's Wort), as they may decrease its effectiveness.

Asundexian is not recommended in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment. It should also be withheld for at least 24 hours before an invasive procedure and for at least 24 hours after thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke, the FDA noted.

Another FXIa inhibitor, milvexian, remains under investigation for secondary stroke prevention.

#5718. Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice

Scientists have uncovered an unexpected connection between diet and cancer treatment. In a surprising finding, certain diets typically considered "unhealthy" or "fattening" actually improved responses to a common form of cancer immunotherapy in mice.

The discovery suggests that the success of cancer treatment may depend not only on which bacteria live in the gut, but also on the foods that help those bacteria thrive.

"There is a synergistic relationship between the bacteria that reside in our GI tract, and the food we eat," said Daniela Quail, Associate Professor in the Department of Physiology and Principal Investigator at the Rosalind & Morris Goodman Cancer Institute.

"Even with the right composition of bacteria in your gut, the foods you eat to nourish those populations can determine whether or not you respond to treatment," said Quail.

Quail co-led the research, which examined how diet influences the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors. These widely used immunotherapy drugs help the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. Other senior researchers involved in the study included McGill scientist Logan Walsh and CR-CHUM collaborators Bertrand Routy and Arielle Elkrief. The findings were published in Nature.

Why Unhealthy Diets Produced Surprising Results

One of the most unexpected discoveries was that some diets associated with weight gain appeared to make immunotherapy more effective, challenging assumptions about the relationship between nutrition and cancer treatment.

"Our findings were surprising because they highlighted a benefit of some obesogenic diets," she said. "That tells us the relationship between diet and cancer treatment is more complex than a simple message to eat healthy and exercise."

However, the researchers emphasize that these results should not encourage cancer patients to consume diets that promote obesity. Excess weight carries established health risks, and the findings do not demonstrate that adopting such diets would improve cancer treatment in humans.

Instead, the scientists want to understand how different foods influence the gut microbiome, the enormous community of trillions of bacteria that inhabit the digestive system. Identifying the mechanisms responsible for the improved treatment responses could eventually help researchers develop safer ways to make cancer immunotherapy more effective.

A New Explanation for Cancer's Obesity Paradox

The investigation grew out of a longstanding puzzle in cancer research known as the "obesity paradox."

Obesity is generally linked to a greater risk of developing cancer and dying from the disease. Yet several studies have found that cancer patients with a higher body mass index (BMI) sometimes respond more favorably to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

To investigate this apparent contradiction, the research team tested 12 different diets in mice. Surprisingly, some diets associated with obesity improved the animals' responses to immunotherapy, even when they were consumed for relatively short periods.

These results suggest that the apparent treatment advantage associated with obesity may not be primarily caused by excess body weight. Instead, the explanation could involve the combined influence of diet and gut bacteria on the immune system.

By uncovering how these interactions affect cancer treatment, researchers hope to identify new approaches that reproduce the beneficial effects without exposing patients to the health risks associated with obesity.

The study, "Diet-microbiome synergy underlies obesity-associated immunotherapy efficacy," was published in Nature by McGill PhD graduate Lysanne Desharnais, Daniela Quail, and their collaborators.

Funding was provided by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Terry Fox Research Institute, the Canada Foundation for Innovation, and philanthropic supporters including La Vie en Rose and the Bachynski Family Foundation.

#5717. ADA Publications Chief Resigns

— The plan for the organization's key journal amid the ongoing boycott is a concern, he says

The vice president of publications at the American Diabetes Association (ADA) has resigned amid the ongoing boycott of the organization.

Christian Kohler, who was with the ADA for 22 years, expressed "profound disappointment" at the overall handling of events at this year's annual meeting in New Orleans, but said in his resignation letter that his "immediate decision" to leave was tied to what's happening at the ADA's flagship journal Diabetes Care.

That includes ADA attempting to bring in interim editors while the majority of the journal's staff participates in the boycott.

"Throughout my nearly three decades in scientific and medical publishing, I have worked to uphold the principles of editorial independence, scientific integrity, transparency, and accountability," Kohler wrote. "Based on that experience, I believe the proposed interim editorial arrangement presents serious ethical, operational, and reputational risks."

In particular, Kohler said he's concerned about how interim staff brought in during the boycott have to perform their duties without an editor in chief who assumes ultimate responsibility for everything in the journal. The absence of a formal process to evaluate interim editors' "suitability for handling the breadth and complexity of research" submitted to the journal is also "problematic," he noted in his letter.

He said he also believes these interim editors are "being placed in an untenable position, one in which their ability to succeed will be severely constrained by circumstances beyond their control, potentially placing their own professional reputations at risk."

The approach to bring in interim editors won't restore confidence in the publication, Kohler added.

"To be clear, I fear it will further undermine the credibility, integrity, and international reputation of Diabetes Care, a journal whose standing has been built over decades through the contributions of dedicated editors, reviewers, authors, and ADA publications staff," he wrote.

In an emailed statement to MedPage Today, the ADA defended its actions on Diabetes Care, noting that its interim editorial board consists of "highly experienced and respected healthcare professionals who have dedicated their careers to caring for people living with diabetes, including endocrinologists, primary care physicians focused on diabetes care, diabetes educators, and more."

ADA added that it is in "conversations with some of the people leading the boycott to schedule a meeting," and that it previously outlined the "next steps that we plan to take to learn and improve based on the facts that came to bear from the review."

Many have criticized the organization's final report on what happened at the annual meeting, taking issue with what it described as perceived threats to "disrupt and protest" the event. That final report also said ADA members who were kicked out of the meeting did not violate its code of conduct, a reversal from an earlier version of the report.

The ADA has lost several leaders in the wake of the annual meeting; Chief Science and Medical Officer Rita Kalyani, MD, and ADA Board Chair James Tai left just before the final report came out. Other resignations came soon after the five researchers were booted from the meeting, including Scientific Sessions Planning Committee Chair Mark Atkinson, PhD, and President-Elect Jennifer Green, MD.

Kohler also said the ADA hasn't yet meaningfully addressed the concerns raised by more than 1,200 people participating in the boycott, which launched in September.

"This is not a frivolous exercise for the boycotters," Kohler told MedPage Today, noting that many of them have spent decades volunteering for ADA programs.

"These are the people ... that ADA leadership should be engaging with most closely to confront the challenges faced by people with diabetes and the scientific and medical communities," he said. "That's not happening."

As the ADA "tries to outrun this storm," he added, it's "missing an opportunity to work with and support the professional community on so many urgent, critical issues."

"My sincere hope is that my letter will play some small role in facilitating a discussion and real action that resolves the boycott," he noted. "I, too, invested a lot in the organization over the years, and I also care deeply about its mission."

Kohler said his resignation would be effective Nov. 30.

#5716. CMS makes it official, codifying Medicare drug price negotiations established under IRA

CMS makes it official, codifying Medicare drug price negotiations established under IRA" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Against a backdrop of repeated industry challenges in court, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) is locking in the drug price negotiation framework established under the Biden-era Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).

In turn, the process under which CMS selects certain high-spend Medicare Part B or Part D drugs and negotiates lower prices with manufacturers will carry on into 2029 and beyond. The rule codifies and expands policies previously established through guidance for the initial 2026-28 period.

The final rule is slated to go into effect Dec. 5, CMS said in a fact sheet accompanying Thursday’s announcement. By Feb. 1 of next year, CMS will select up to 20 drugs covered under Medicare Part B or Part D for price negotiations taking effect in 2029, with the potential to also select medicines included in previous rounds for renegotiation.

That upcoming group of drugs will make up the fourth cycle of pricing negotiations, with negotiated prices taking effect in 2029. CMS asserted that the rule gives both patients and drugmakers “a clear path forward as the agency builds on the program’s results and continues negotiating prices for high-cost drugs.”

The initial rounds of price negotiations have already included a slew of prominent brands, including Novo's semaglutide franchise of Wegovy and Ozempic and cancer meds like Bristol Myers Squibb’s Pomalyst, Pfizer’s Ibrance and AstraZeneca’s Calquence.

Meanwhile, the latest tranche of drugs selected earlier this year for negotiation, whose new prices would go into effect in 2028, includes notable entrants like Gilead’s HIV treatment Biktarvy, AbbVie’s Botox and Eli Lilly’s diabetes drug Trulicity, to name just a few.

Beyond codifying the framework for price negotiations in 2029 and subsequent years, CMS has also taken steps to fine-tune several elements of the program.

Namely, the rule finalizes a policy on how CMS classifies certain fixed-combination drugs, with the aim of addressing “potential program integrity concerns” that could encourage drugmakers to evade negotiated prices by steering patients toward new product formulations.

The rule also includes a provision establishing a temporary “small biotech floor” that prevents CMS from offering or accepting a counteroffer below a specified price floor for certain eligible small biotech drugs in 2029 and 2030. It also codifies two policies related to Medicare Part D intended to ensure plan coverage of medicines with a maximum fair price in effect and limit the prices plans pay pharmacies and other dispensing entities.

The IRA and the Medicare price negotiations it empowered have been frequent targets of the biopharma industry, which has broadly alleged that the policy is unconstitutional and that the pricing talks aren’t as voluntary as advertised. But attempts by major drugmakers and powerful trade organizations like the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) to push back on Medicare price negotiations have repeatedly stalled out.

In the interim, the U.S. government has made a separate and more recent push to rein in high prescription drug costs by leaning on President Donald Trump’s “most favored nation” (MFN) strategy.

“President Trump directed us to lower drug costs for Americans using every tool at our disposal,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., said in a statement announcing the new rule. “This rule provides additional tools to help CMS negotiate better deals, achieve greater savings for taxpayers and beneficiaries, and improve health outcomes for seniors who rely on the Medicare Prescription Drug Program.”

MFN, for its part, has yielded at times, controversial deals with more than two dozen drugmakers, generally involving commitments to price new medicines in line with prices in high-income comparator countries and offer MFN pricing on certain existing drugs through Medicaid.

Through those deals, which have also included investment commitments in the U.S., drugmakers have been able to secure temporary exemptions from the Trump administration’s threatened pharmaceutical import tariffs.

Around this week’s midterm elections, several Big Pharma executives have signaled that they expect little immediate change to their thinking around MFN. Nevertheless, the lack of transparency surrounding the deals has already drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers. With Democrats set to control both chambers of Congress beginning in January, the party may soon press harder to uncover the details of those agreements.

#5715. Another Option for Rare Benign Soft-Tissue Tumor Wins FDA Approval

— Pimicotinib achieved 54% objective response rate in unresectable tenosynovial giant cell tumor

The FDA approved the small-molecule inhibitor pimicotinib (Pimjetmi) for selected patients with symptomatic tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT) and high surgical risk.

An oral selective inhibitor of colony stimulating factor-1 receptor (CSF-1R), pimicotinib is indicated for TGCT for which surgery might cause worsening functional limitation or severe morbidity. Pimicotinib is the third FDA-approved drug for TGCT, joining two other CSF-1R inhibitors, vimseltinib (Romvimza), approved in 2025, and pexidartinib (Turalio), approved in 2019.

TGCT is a rare, locally aggressive soft-tissue tumor that primarily affects otherwise healthy younger (median age 38) adults. The condition originates in the joint synovium, bursae, or tendon sheaths and has the potential to cause substantial functional limitation and morbidity. Surgery is the primary treatment when feasible.

Primary support for the approval came from the phase III MANEUVER trial. Investigators in Asia, Europe, and North America randomized 94 patients with unresectable TGCT 2:1 to pimicotinib or placebo. The trial met the primary endpoint of objective response rate (ORR) at week 25. The primary analysis showed an ORR of 54% with pimicotinib and 3% with placebo (P<0.0001).

Recently reported 2-year results from the trial showed durable responses with pimicotinib (76-78% at 2 years), along with improvements in pain, stiffness, and range of motion.

"For people living with TGCT, the impact of the disease is often felt through persistent limitations in mobility, physical function, and the ability to carry out everyday activities," investigator Vinod Ravi, MD, of the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, said last month in a press release from drugmaker EMD Serono announcing those results.

"What is encouraging about these 2-year findings is the consistency of improvements, not only in the durability of tumor response, but across the symptoms and functional outcomes that matter to patients," added Ravi. "Together with the observed safety profile, these results provide important insight into the potential for pimicotinib to deliver meaningful benefit over time."

According to the FDA, the most common adverse reactions in the pimicotinib arm (>20% of patients) were pruritus, rash, facial and periorbital edema, fatigue, nausea, headache, and peripheral edema. Laboratory abnormalities occurring in more than 30% of patients consisted of increased creatine phosphokinase, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase, lipase, cholesterol, amylase, and alanine aminotransferase.

Pimicotinib was approved earlier this year in Canada and Switzerland and in China in 2025.

#5714. A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms

A simple blood test could help identify people at increased risk of Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline years before they experience any noticeable problems with memory or thinking. In a large international study, researchers found that older adults with very high levels of a particular blood biomarker faced a 38% chance of developing cognitive impairment within five years. Over 10 years, the estimated risk rose to 78%, although the longer-term findings were based on substantially less data.

The findings offer new insight into the potential of blood tests to predict future cognitive problems in people who currently show no signs of impairment. The research was led by scientists at the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute and involved teams working across three continents. The results were presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference and simultaneously published in JAMA.

The study focused on phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), a blood biomarker associated with Alzheimer's disease. A test measuring this marker recently received federal clearance, raising hopes that blood testing could make Alzheimer's detection more accessible. However, an important question has remained: Can these tests reliably predict whether someone with normal cognitive function will eventually develop symptoms?

Blood Test Reveals Cognitive Decline Risk Years in Advance

To investigate, researchers combined information from six observational studies and clinical trials conducted in North America, Japan, and Australia. Together, these studies included 2,684 older adults who showed no signs of cognitive impairment when they entered the research.

At enrollment, participants provided blood samples that were analyzed for p-tau217. They also underwent positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans, allowing researchers to establish baseline measurements of brain health. Annual follow-up assessments were then used to monitor changes in memory, thinking, and other cognitive abilities.

The combined data covered an unusually long period. Some participants entered one of the studies as early as 2004, while the most recent follow-up assessments took place in 2025.

Across the studies, approximately 478 participants eventually developed cognitive impairment. When researchers compared these outcomes with the original blood test results, they found a strong relationship between higher p-tau217 levels and the likelihood of future cognitive problems.

Among people with very high biomarker levels, the estimated probability of developing cognitive impairment reached 38% within five years. By 10 years, that figure increased to 78%. However, the researchers emphasized that substantially fewer observations were available for the 10-year period and beyond, making those longer-term predictions less certain.

A Powerful Alzheimer's Predictor Beyond Genetics and Brain Scans

One of the most important findings was that p-tau217 provided information about future cognitive decline beyond what could be explained by other established risk factors.

The biomarker remained significantly associated with cognitive impairment even after researchers accounted for amyloid-beta plaques, which are abnormal protein deposits in the brain that can be detected with PET imaging. Its predictive value also extended beyond known genetic risk factors (such as APOE4).

This suggests that a relatively simple blood test could eventually provide doctors with additional information when estimating an individual's likelihood of developing cognitive difficulties.

"This is a critical step toward better understanding what p-tau217 can tell us about a person's risk for cognitive impairment," said lead author Rachel F. Buckley, PhD, a cognitive neuroscientist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "What really sets this work apart is that it estimates an individual's level of risk for cognitive impairment. We harmonized data across six cohorts, creating a large and varied data set, and still found consistent results showing how p-tau217 informs risk over time."

Rather than simply identifying biological changes associated with Alzheimer's, the research helps estimate how those changes translate into the probability of developing symptoms over a specific period.

Why Alzheimer's Blood Tests Are Not Yet Recommended for Healthy People

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that blood tests are not currently recommended for routine Alzheimer's risk screening in people without symptoms.

One major reason is that preventive treatments capable of changing the course of the disease have not yet been established for otherwise healthy individuals identified as being at elevated risk.

"We do not yet have disease-modifying treatments for people who find out they are at high risk for developing cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease, which is why we don't recommend currently available blood tests for asymptomatic individuals. Today, our medical advice would remain the same regardless of test results: exercise regularly, maintain a healthy diet, and prioritize sleep and overall wellness," said senior and corresponding author Reisa Sperling, MD, a neurologist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "But the preventive care landscape could change rapidly if ongoing trials of disease-modifying therapies prove beneficial. In the future, these tests could help identify those who might benefit most from these treatments. Our long-term goal is to get us to where cholesterol testing is in predicting your risk of a heart attack."

There are also important limitations to the research. Although the investigators brought together data from multiple studies and geographic regions, the participants may not fully represent the broader population. This potential selection bias could affect how well the findings apply to other groups.

In addition, the analysis focused on predicting cognitive impairment over relatively limited periods rather than estimating a person's lifetime risk. Researchers say larger, more representative studies and longer follow-up periods will be needed to confirm the findings and improve the precision of individual risk predictions.

Could Blood Tests Help Prevent Alzheimer's Before Symptoms Begin?

The greatest potential benefit of this approach may emerge as scientists develop treatments designed to slow or prevent Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline before noticeable symptoms develop.

Several clinical trials are already investigating whether disease-modifying therapies can benefit people who have biological signs of Alzheimer's but have not yet experienced cognitive impairment. If those treatments prove effective, blood biomarkers such as p-tau217 could help identify individuals most likely to benefit from early intervention.

Such an approach could eventually make Alzheimer's prevention more similar to cardiovascular prevention, where cholesterol measurements help doctors estimate future heart attack risk and determine who may benefit from treatment.

For now, the blood test offers researchers a way to identify higher-risk individuals who may be suitable candidates for prevention studies.

"Today, p-tau217 can help identify people at high risk for future Alzheimer's dementia for participation in prevention trials," said Sperling. "As these trials move forward, individualized estimates, including the biomarker's prognostic value, could guide earlier treatment and monitoring decisions."

Authorship: In addition to Sperling and Buckley, Mass General Brigham authors include Diana L. Townsend, Colin J. Birkenbihl, Madison Cuppels, Gillian T. Coughlan, Mabel T. Seto, Jane A. Brown, Michael J. Properzi, Merle C. Hönig, Annie Li, Aaron P. #5713. Hims & Hers inks deal with Eli Lilly to offer branded weight loss drugs

Hims & Hers inks deal with Eli Lilly to offer branded weight loss drugs" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hims & Hers struck a deal with Eli Lilly to offer the drugmaker’s branded obesity treatments through its online health and wellness platform.

Under the agreement, Eli Lilly will give Hims & Hers pharmacies direct access to its U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved GLP-1 medications at self-pay prices. Eligible patients on the Hims & Hers platform can be prescribed and order Eli Lilly's injectable Zepbound (tirzepatide) and daily oral medication Foundayo (orforglipron) without leaving the company's platform.

Prior to this agreement, Lilly drugs were available to patients on Hims & Hers only if they left the site and went to Lilly's direct-to-consumer platform, LillyDirect.

Shares of Hims & Hers jumped 8% Friday following news of the Eli Lilly partnership.

The agreement brings together Lilly’s obesity medicines and Hims & Hers’ consumer platform to expand consumers' access to FDA-approved weight loss drugs, the companies said.

"Patients can complete a consultation, receive a prescription if their provider determines it is appropriate and have an FDA-approved Lilly medicine shipped directly to their home, all in one seamless experience," the companies said in a press release.

Self-pay pricing starts at $149 per month for Foundayo and $299 per month for Zepbound.

"At Lilly, we are always looking for new ways to help more people get the medicines they need, and that means meeting patients where they already are," said Ilya Yuffa, executive vice president and president, Lilly USA and global customer capabilities, Eli Lilly and Company, in a statement. "Millions of people turn to Hims & Hers for their care, and through this agreement, those patients now have a simple, more direct way to get FDA-approved Lilly medicine at an affordable price if prescribed."

Hims & Hers' technology platform supports provider outreach, follow-up care and treatment planning. Weight loss patients on Hims & Hers receive a membership experience that includes 24/7 access to a care team, nutrition guidance, regular clinical check-ins and access to the Hims & Hers Weight Loss community, according to the company.

The agreement with Eli Lilly mirrors Hims & Hers' partnership with Novo Nordisk, which has been selling its branded weight loss drugs Wegovy and Ozempic through Hims & Hers since March. Novo had previously sued the telehealth company for offering compounded versions of its medications. Hims & Hers' agreement with Novo marked a shift in its obesity strategy toward FDA-approved branded GLP-1 treatments and away from cheaper compounded GLP-1 drugs.

Earlier this year, Hims & Hers took heat from the pharmaceutical manufacturer and federal regulators after announcing plans to launch a knockoff of Novo's oral pill. It backed down from those plans under pressure.

Hims & Hers stated that it never offered access to compounded copies of Lilly’s GLP-1 drugs and has committed not to do so in the future.

As part of the agreement, the companies have committed to protecting independent clinical decision-making, so that providers on the Hims & Hers platform continue to prescribe the treatment they determine is right for each patient.

“Lilly is one of the most innovative pharmaceutical companies in history, and I’m incredibly proud that Hims & Hers is a part of making sure more people can access the medicines they’ve created,” said Andrew Dudum, co-founder and CEO of Hims & Hers, in a statement. “By working together, we’re not just reaching more people with obesity with seamless, personal access to FDA-approved Lilly medicine. We’re showing the industry what innovators can achieve for customers everywhere when we work together to make the world well.”

Hims & Hers has faced financial pressure as it shifts from high-margin compounded GLP-1s to lower-margin branded weight-loss drugs. The company posted a $92 million loss in Q1, including $33 million in restructuring costs, largely from write-downs of its compounded GLP-1 supply chain, which executives said faced “risk of obsolescence.”

In Q2, Hims & Hers reported an $86 million loss, compared with a $43 million profit a year earlier. The quarter included $81 million in one-time costs, including expenses tied to its exit from compounded GLP-1s.

#5711. Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day

Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function.

Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes.

"The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," says Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake."

Daily Peanuts Linked to Better Memory and Brain Blood Flow

The study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them.

The new findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%.

Cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an important indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition.

How Scientists Measured the Effects of Peanuts on the Brain

One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology.

To examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose.

The team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests.

Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible.

"Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," says Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance."

What Participants Ate During the 16-Week Study

To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period.

Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals.

During the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches.

The study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center.

Funding was provided by The Peanut Institute Foundation. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript.

#5710. What Is a Great Google Quality Real Estate Score: A Comprehensive Guide

Navigating the world of Google Ads can be challenging, especially in an industry as competitive as real estate. One term you've probably heard in relation to Google Ads is "Quality Score." #5708. Anthropic launches Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 with science, coding upgrades

Anthropic PBC today pulled back the curtains on Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, its two most capable large language models to date.

The LLMs are identical as far as their core capabilities are concerned. The difference is that Fable 5.2 blocks certain biology and cybersecurity use cases, while Mythos 5.2 includes more relaxed guardrails. The latter model is only available to trusted researchers through a pair of limited-access programs.

Anthropic tested Fable 5.2 against its predecessor across 14 artificial intelligence benchmarks. The model beat Fable 5.1’s score by more than 10% across most of the tests. It’s particularly adept at scientific research: Fable 5.2 scored 74.6% on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, a 22% improvement over Fable 5.1.

Earlier this year, Anthropic used an unreleased LLM to generate a computer-verifiable version of a famous mathematical proof. The project took 11 days. According to Anthropic, Fable 5.2 reduced the workflow to 30 hours by spinning up 1,000 agents to parallelize calculations. In a separate project, it answered two open questions about a theoretical physics concept related to black holes.

The company also tested Mythos 5.2, the invite-only version of Fable 5.2. It asked the model to study the protective shells of harmless viruses called AAVs. AAV shells, or capsids as they’re known in scientific parlance, are used by some therapies to deliver drugs.

Mythos 5.2 accurately modeled the structure of 28 out of the 34 AAV capsids it studied. The result is notable because capsids comprise dozens of different proteins. Other cutting-edge models that are optimized for biology research, notably Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold2, can only model the structure of individual proteins. The creators of the latter model won one half of the 2024 Nobel Prize in chemistry.

Fable 5.2 includes guardrails that block most research biology questions and many cybersecurity-related prompts. If users enter a request that falls into either of those categories, the model sends it to Opus 4.8 or Opus 5. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 is 55% less likely to erroneously block safe prompts than Fable 5.1.

The model outperforms its predecessor by more than 13% across two coding benchmarks called FrontierCode 2.0 FrontierSWE 2.0. According to Anthropic, one of its engineers put the model’s programming capabilities to the test by asking it to build an operating system. Fable 5.2 spun up up 1,000 agents that completed the task in about eight days. The operating system they created can run on a laptop, offers network access and features a Claude sidebar.

Anthropic sees customers using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 to speed up highly complicated, open-ended technical tasks. The company says more day-to-day workflows can be automated more efficiently using Opus 5.5, an LLM it introduced in July. Users can also combine the models by having Opus 5.5 ask Fable 5.2 or Mythos 5.2 for advise when it encounters a bottleneck.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. That makes them 20% more affordable than Anthropic’s previous-generation models. Both LLMs offer a high-performance mode that generates prompt responses 2.5 times faster than the standard tier for double the price.

#5707. Scientists discover a hidden driver of high cholesterol and a way to stop it

Heart disease linked to high cholesterol continues to be the leading cause of death worldwide. Although doctors have more treatment options than ever, many people still struggle to lower their cholesterol to safe levels. Others experience side effects that make existing medications difficult to take.

Researchers at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine have now identified a previously unknown biological pathway that helps explain why diets high in cholesterol can gradually weaken the body's ability to remove harmful low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol from the bloodstream. Even more promising, they have identified an experimental drug that has already undergone safety testing in humans and could potentially interfere with this process.

The findings, published in Nature, could open the door to a new approach to treating high cholesterol.

"We've known for a long time that a high-cholesterol diet reduces the liver's ability to clear cholesterol from the blood, but we didn't fully understand why," said senior author Alan Saltiel, PhD, professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine and director of the UC San Diego/UCLA Diabetes Research Center. "This new discovery explains a critical piece of that puzzle."

The liver plays a central role in controlling cholesterol levels. It removes cholesterol from the bloodstream so it can be processed, broken down, and used by other parts of the body.

To accomplish this, liver cells rely on structures called LDL receptors. Located on the surface of these cells, the receptors work much like docking stations, capturing LDL cholesterol circulating in the blood and bringing it inside for processing.

The number of available receptors matters. When liver cells have more LDL receptors, they can remove more cholesterol from circulation. This is one reason widely used cholesterol medications, including statins and PCSK9 inhibitors, are effective. They help maintain or increase the number of receptors available to clear LDL cholesterol.

Scientists Uncover a Hidden Cholesterol Pathway

Using experiments involving mice and human cells, the researchers discovered a previously unrecognized process that interferes with the liver's ability to clear cholesterol. Over time, this mechanism reduces the number of LDL receptors, making it harder for the body to keep blood cholesterol under control.

The process begins with a protein known as Ral, which Saltiel had previously investigated in fat cells. The team discovered that consuming high amounts of dietary cholesterol activates Ral, setting off a chain of events that leads to the loss of LDL receptors. As Ral activity increases, fewer receptors remain available to remove harmful cholesterol from the bloodstream.

The researchers then identified another critical piece of the mechanism: an enzyme called cathepsin A (CTSA). This enzyme helps drive the process responsible for depleting LDL receptors.

When scientists used a small molecule inhibitor to block CTSA, the results were striking. LDL receptors became more stable, and levels of circulating LDL cholesterol dropped dramatically in mice.

The discovery is especially significant because the newly identified pathway is different from those targeted by current cholesterol medications. That distinction could make it possible to develop treatments for patients who do not respond adequately to existing drugs.

"There's still a real need for new cholesterol-lowering options, since some people can't get to safe levels even with the drugs we have now," said Saltiel. "This new pathway we discovered is completely separate from anything that existing drugs target, so it gives us a new opportunity to fill that gap."

A Previously Tested Drug Could Accelerate Treatment

Discovering a new biological target is usually only the beginning of a lengthy drug development process. Researchers often need years of additional work to identify a suitable compound and determine whether it can be used safely in people.

In this case, however, the scientists may already have a promising candidate.

A drug designed to inhibit CTSA had previously been developed as a potential treatment for heart failure. Although the program was eventually discontinued for strategic reasons, the experimental medication had already progressed through a Phase 1 clinical trial, where it was successfully evaluated for safety in humans.

That earlier work could provide an important advantage. Rather than beginning drug development from scratch, researchers believe the existing CTSA inhibitor may be ready to advance into a Phase 2 clinical trial to investigate its effectiveness against high cholesterol.

The findings are still at an early stage, and the drug has not yet been shown to lower cholesterol in humans. Nevertheless, its previous clinical testing could shorten the path toward determining whether this new treatment strategy works in patients.

"Luckily, there's an experimental drug sitting on the shelf that's already been shown to be safe in humans," said Saltiel. "We hope to test whether this might be effective by conducting a clinical trial -- which could potentially bring a new treatment option to patients much sooner than would have been expected."

Co-authors of the study include Xue Feng, Shuo Zhang, Yuqi Wang, Twisha Kurlagunda, Allyssa Sit, Sadatsugu Sakane, Se Yong Park, Churaibhon Wisessaowapak, Kaylee Nguyen, Jamie Yan, Himani Pothulu, Catherine Dinh, Felicia Chu, Yuyao Ren, Bichen Zhang, Patrick Secrest, Chao-Wei Hung, Preethi Veeragandham, Yuliya Skorobogatko, Tatiana Kisseleva, and Amit R. Majithia at UC San Diego; Priya Jaishankar, Pusu Yang, and Adam Renslo at the University of California, San Francisco; Linmeng Han and Peng Zhao at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio; and Philip L.S.M. Gordts at the University of Utah.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health (Grants P30DK063491, R01DK117551, R01DK128796, and R01DK135289) and an American Diabetes Association postdoctoral fellowship (1-25-PDF-76).

#5706. GLP-1 Pill Shows Benefit in Sleep Apnea

— If approved, orforglipron could become the first oral treatment for obstructive sleep apnea

The oral GLP-1 receptor agonist orforglipron (Foundayo) improved sleep-disordered breathing in patients with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea and overweight or obesity, two phase III trials showed.

For the treatment regimen estimand, mean change of apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) was significantly improved from baseline to week 52 with orforglipron compared with placebo both in patients receiving continuous positive airway pressure (PAP; -17.3 vs -5.3 events/hour, P<0.001) and in patients not receiving PAP (-17.8 vs -4.5 events/hour, P<0.001).

Orforglipron also showed significant improvements in secondary outcomes, including the sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, as well as reductions in body weight, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, and blood pressure, reported Vaishnavi Kundel, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

"These data support the potential use of orforglipron as a promising oral treatment option for moderate-to-severe OSA [obstructive sleep apnea] in adults with obesity or overweight," Kundel said at the American Heart Association (AHA) annual meeting held in Chicago.

AHA commenter Michael Grandner, PhD, from the University of Arizona in Tucson, said having an oral option to treat obstructive sleep apnea would be "game-changing."

"As a reminder, to treat sleep apnea right now, we have instruments that work really well, but they can be complicated and difficult to use," Grandner said. "Not only is it undertreated, but among those who are treated, use is relatively low. This might help get people toward the treatment that they need."

The results of the ATTAIN-OSA trials were published simultaneously in JAMA.

Orforglipron is a small-molecule, non-peptide oral GLP-1 receptor agonist that has already received FDA approval for weight management.

In an editorial accompanying the publication, Diego Mazzotti, PhD, and Damien Stevens, MD, both of the University of Kansas Medical Center in Kansas City, pointed out that for patients with severe disease, "it is expected that orforglipron will be one component of a broader treatment plan."

They suggested that pragmatic trials comparing and combining orforglipron with PAP, oral appliances, tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound), or other treatments are needed. "For many years, individuals with OSA had few alternatives when PAP was inadequate," they wrote. "Orforglipron adds an oral option to a growing number of treatments from which clinicians and patients can select and work together to build better individualized care."

AHA discussant for the presentation, Ildiko Lingvay, MD, MPH, of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, compared the results for orforglipron to those reported for another GLP-1 drug, tirzepatide, which is already approved for obstructive sleep apnea.

She pointed to apparent advantages for tirzepatide over orforglipron in terms of obstructive sleep apnea disease control, with greater improvement in AHI as well as in hypoxic burden, and in safety measures. Cardiovascular risk reduction is also not yet established with orforglipron, while tirzepatide is already FDA-approved for cardiovascular risk reduction in people with diabetes.

"The biggest benefit of orforglipron is really the fact that it comes in a tablet form, for once-daily administration, while tirzepatide requires a cold chain supply and injections," Lingvay noted. "The take-home message is that orforglipron is the first ever oral therapy to have shown improvements in disordered breathing as well as beneficial effects on cardiovascular risk factors, and that includes weight, systolic blood pressure, and inflammatory markers."

The ATTAIN-OSA program included two 52-week, phase III, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials involving patients on PAP (N=349) or not on PAP (N=363). The studies were carried out at 66 sites in the U.S., Argentina, Brazil, China, the Czech Republic, Germany, Japan, Mexico, and Taiwan.

Adults with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea and a body mass index of 27 or higher were eligible. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either once-daily orforglipron at the maximum tolerated dose, equivalent to a 9-, 14.5-, or 17.2-mg tablet dose, or placebo.

Gastrointestinal events were the most commonly reported adverse events, occurring in 68% of patients on orforglipron versus 37.4% of those on placebo among the trial participants not on PAP, and in 70.6% of those on orforglipron versus 36.6% of those on placebo in the PAP trial.

#5705. Doximity expands clinical AI footprint to more than 190 health systems

Doximity expands clinical AI footprint to more than 190 health systems" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Doximity is rapidly expanding its clinical AI footprint with health systems, with more than 190 organizations having now purchased its AI suite, up from 165 organizations last quarter.

Those health system customers include 10 of the nation's top 20 hospitals, Doximity executives said during the company's fiscal 2027 second-quarter earnings call on Thursday.

NewYork-Presbyterian has integrated Doximity’s AI tools directly into its electronic health record (EHR) workflow. The partnership grants clinicians across NewYork-Presbyterian, Columbia University Irving Medical Center and Weill Cornell Medicine frictionless access to AI tools, including Doximity Scribe and Doximity Ask, the company's AI-powered clinical decision support tool.

NewYork-Presbyterian rolled out Doximity’s AI suite to clinicians across 10 hospitals and hundreds of locations. The deployment builds on NYP’s use of Doximity for video and phone visits since 2021.

UCSD Health is one of the first hospitals to adopt Doximity's new patient context feature, which allows AI to ingest EHR charts, labs, and patient history directly to give patient-specific answers and guideline-based treatment plans, Jeff Tangney, Doximity CEO, said during the earnings call.

"Our patient context feature is now available for thousands of doctors, and they're writing prompts half as long, 12 words versus our 24-word average, because they no longer have to retype the chart details into a search bar. Our AI already has the labs, notes, and problem list, so it can find the pertinent clinical details deep in their record," Tangney said.

The company is also opening API access to its clinical intelligence layer to expand to more workflows.

Tangney stressed that Doximity is focused on offering clinicians a full clinical AI suite across workflows including telehealth, AI documentation, scheduling, clinical questions, patient context and clinical evidence.

"We offer them a suite, not a search bar," Tangney said. "That suite allows them to do the telehealth visit, to have notes taken on that visit, what we call Scribe, and then to ask questions about that visit with the patient context."

Doximity is a digital platform for U.S. medical professionals that offers workflow tools such as a telehealth solution, a clinician-to-patient dialer tool and digital faxing capabilities. The company aims to become a leading AI platform for doctors with plans to scale its clinical AI suite, including its ambient note-taking tool Scribe and clinical AI assistant and medical search engine Ask. A year ago, Doximity acquired clinical AI company Pathway and then integrated Pathway's datasets and its AI into its free Doximity GPT product to offer DoxGPT (now Ask).

Doximity is leaning hard into AI accuracy and safety as AI adoption rapidly grows. AI accuracy "is the number one concern doctors have about AI," Tangney told investors and analysts on the call. "AI deals in probabilities. Patient care demands precision," he said.

The company is making clinical reliability a major part of its competitive positioning. Doximity recently launched DoseCheck, a deterministic verifier for medication safety. Through a partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health, the company embedded UpToDate's evidence-based clinical content directly within Doximity Ask.

"Every clinical AI model has read the National Library of Medicine, which has all of the journals and guidelines, but Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate stands alone as the proprietary gold standard reference for point of care. Their 7,600 physician authors provide unique advice about what to do when there is not an RCT, or randomized controlled trial, to answer the question," Tangney said.

The partnership with UpToDate represents a "strong synergy of Doximity's AI evidence tools and [UpToDate's] unique expert opinion and physician expertise," he noted.

UpToDate has 2,500 health systems as clients, compared to Doximity's 190, and that creates "additional synergies" for the company, Tangney said. Doximity plans to expand its relationship with UpToDate, he noted: "It's the beginning of what we think will be a very strategic, long-term partnership," he added.

Physician AI engagement is growing quickly, according to the company.  Doximity said quarterly active workflow prescribers increased 34% year over year, accelerating from the prior quarter. Approximately half of the 1.8 million U.S. prescribers, roughly 900,000 clinicians, used Doximity workflow products during the quarter. The company sees continued growth in telehealth and scheduling alongside rapidly expanding use of AI and patient-specific clinical tools, Tangney said.

A year ago, the company's workflow active-user growth was in the single digits versus 34% now, Matt Sonefeldt, Doximity's chief financial officer, said during the call. Doximity is investing heavily in AI. Rapid growth in clinician engagement, particularly with the company's workflow tools, is laying the groundwork for greater monetization and business growth over the next several years, Sonefeldt said.

Doximity reported $174.5 million in revenue during the quarter ending September 30, up 4% year over year, beating guidance. Adjusted EBITDA was $89 million, or a 51% margin, despite AI spending growing more than sixfold year over year.

The company reported net income of $34.7 million, versus $62.1 million a year ago, representing a margin of 19.9%, versus 36.8%. And the company reported adjusted EPS of 36 cents per share.

The company's Q2 results beat Wall Street analysts' estimates as analysts expected revenue of $170.8 million, adjusted EBITDA of $81 million and adjusted EPS of 35 cents per share.

Doximity raised its full-year revenue outlook to $678 million to $683 million, about 6% growth at the midpoint. For the full year, the company expects adjusted EBITDA between $317 million and $325 million.

The company launched its commercial AI Search product for pharmaceutical companies in late April, and it's gaining traction with pharmaceutical advertisers, executives said. Sixteen of the top 20 companies have purchased it, with three more in contracting, and bookings have reached eight figures, Sonefeldt said. AI Search revenue will ramp up gradually through calendar 2027, he noted.

AI monetization is coming from the pharma side and selling AI Search as an advertising product, Sonefeldt noted. "We do sell AI as a separate enterprise agreement to health systems customers. We charge a nominal amount as part of our broader workflow suite. As we think about this going forward, we see the primary monetization engine being on the pharma side of our business, specifically through the ad products that we sell," he told analysts during a Q&A on the call.

On the clinical side, Doximity aims to build a trusted AI workflow layer that physicians use for documentation, clinical questions, patient-specific decision support, telehealth and communication. On the commercial side, the company sees opportunities to turn that engagement and clinical intent into a new advertising and search business serving pharma.

"With AI Search now available to our pharma clients, we're growing into a much larger market," Tangney told analysts and investors. "We think we're entering a whole new market here, which has historically been paid search."

Doximity is trying to capture marketing dollars that historically went to Google and other search channels. Tangney cited an estimated $14 billion spent annually by pharma on paid search in the U.S.

The company also plans to introduce biddable or auction-based purchasing, which would make the product look much more like conventional paid search.

Shares of Doximity slumped following its Thursday evening earnings report as investors reacted to significant margin compression, Yahoo Finance reported. Doximity's stock is down nearly 25% this year.

"On the stock, while shares have shed roughly a quarter of value year-to-date due to lingering questions about AI threats and the uncertain backdrop for pharma marketing spend, solid results such as these, along with positive commentary around macro factors should continue to power the recovery that has been ongoing since the fiscal first-quarter earnings print," Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote in an analyst note.

"We continue to be optimistic on Doximity's competitive position, with robust growth in utilization metrics and novel AI offerings launching to pharma partners. Continued development of AI-based workflow solutions should support Doximity’s ability to remain a share gainer in healthcare professional (HCP) marketing, supporting long-term growth above market averages," Daniels wrote.

#5703. Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer

Scientists at the University of Virginia Comprehensive Cancer Center have developed a promising experimental strategy for treating glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive malignant brain tumor in adults. The new approach could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles that have limited the effectiveness of existing brain cancer treatments.

The research team, led by UVA's Roger Abounader, MD, PhD, identified tiny genetic molecules known as "microRNAs" that can interfere with several genes responsible for the development and growth of glioblastoma. To deliver these molecules into the brain, the researchers combined specialized nanoparticles, focused ultrasound and microscopic bubbles. Together, these technologies offer a way to temporarily cross the brain's protective barrier, which normally prevents many treatments from reaching brain tumors and other neurological conditions.

"This new approach could help target numerous molecules that promote cancer growth, including those for which no drugs exist, at the same time to achieve better therapies," said Abounader, a professor at UVA's School of Medicine in the Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Cancer Biology, as well as its Comprehensive Cancer Center and Center for RNA Science and Medicine. "We are hoping to translate our findings into future clinical trials for patients with glioblastoma and other brain tumors."

Why Glioblastoma Is So Difficult to Treat

Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults and one of the most aggressive forms of cancer. It claims more than 13,000 lives in the United States each year. One reason it is so difficult to treat is that cancer cells spread into surrounding healthy brain tissue, making it nearly impossible for surgeons to remove the entire tumor.

Another major challenge is the brain's natural "blood-brain barrier." This protective system helps shield the brain from harmful substances, including toxins and infectious agents. Unfortunately, it also blocks many drugs that could otherwise be used to attack brain cancer.

Current treatment generally begins with surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible. Patients then receive radiation therapy and chemotherapy to help control the remaining cancer and extend survival. Despite these efforts, glioblastoma remains exceptionally difficult to manage.

The UVA researchers are pursuing a different strategy. Instead of relying on drugs that target individual cancer-related processes, their approach uses microRNAs, small pieces of genetic material capable of suppressing the activity of multiple problematic genes at the same time.

By disrupting several genes that help glioblastoma grow and survive, the treatment could potentially slow or even stop tumor growth. This ability to target multiple cancer-driving mechanisms is especially important because combining several conventional cancer drugs can produce harmful side effects. In addition, many of the molecules involved in cancer growth cannot currently be targeted by available medications.

Using Ultrasound to Deliver Cancer-Fighting Molecules

Getting these genetic molecules into the brain presents another major challenge. To overcome it, Abounader's team uses focused ultrasound guided by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), allowing researchers to direct sound waves precisely toward the intended area.

The ultrasound works with tiny "microbubbles" to temporarily open the blood-brain barrier. This creates a brief opportunity for nanoparticles carrying the microRNAs to pass through the barrier and enter the brain, where they can act on genes involved in tumor growth.

The researchers tested this approach in laboratory experiments and animal models of glioblastoma. Their findings showed that the microRNA treatment slowed tumor growth and helped the animals survive longer.

Although these results are encouraging, the strategy remains experimental and will require additional research before it can be evaluated in human patients. Abounader believes the findings provide an important early indication that the technology could eventually benefit people with glioblastoma and potentially those with other types of cancer.

"This approach could have broad applications for several brain and other human diseases," Abounader said. "We and many others are intensively working to lighten the burden of cancer, and hopefully also completely cure it, but this requires a continued investment in cancer and medical research."

UVA Expands Focused Ultrasound Cancer Research

UVA Health has been at the forefront of focused ultrasound research since the technology's early development. Over the years, its scientists have built an extensive research program investigating how precisely directed sound waves might be used to treat a wide range of medical conditions.

Recognizing the technology's potential in cancer care, UVA partnered with the Charlottesville-based Focused Ultrasound Foundation to establish the Focused Ultrasound Immuno-Oncology (FUSION) Center. It is the first center in the world devoted specifically to investigating how focused ultrasound can be combined with cancer immunotherapy. Researchers believe this combination could lead to major advances in cancer treatment during the 21st century.

The effort also supports the broader missions of UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center and UVA's Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology, both of which are working to improve care through new medical discoveries.

UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center is among just 57 cancer centers nationwide to receive the National Cancer Institute's prestigious "comprehensive" designation. The recognition reflects its excellence in cancer research and patient care.

The Manning Institute was established to speed the discovery and development of new medicines and potential cures for some of the most difficult diseases. Its work is supported by a statewide clinical trials network designed to make emerging treatments more accessible to patients as they move through research and testing.

Abounader and his colleagues published their experimental approach and initial laboratory findings in JCI, the Journal of Clinical Investigation. The study is open access and can be read free of charge.

The research team included Shekhar Saha, Ying Zhang, Myron K. Gibert Jr., Collin Dube, Farina Hanif, Elizabeth Qian Xu Mulcahy, Sylwia Bednarek, Yunan Sun, Pawel Marcinkiewicz, Xiantao Wang, Gijung Kwak, Ahsan H. Polash, Haolin Li, Kadie Hudson, Manikarna Dinda, Tapas Saha, Matthew McCord, Fadila Guessous, Nichola Cruickshanks, Rossymar Rivera Colon, Lily Dell'Olio, Rajitha Anbu, Wenjie Liu, Songy Choi, Benjamin Kefas, Pankaj Kumar, Alexander L. Klibanov, David Schiff, Jung Soo Suk, Justin Hanes, Jamie Mata, Markus Hafner and Abounader. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.

Funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Cancer Institute through grants U01 CA220841 and P30 CA044579, along with the NIH's National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke through grants R01 NS122222 and R21 NS122136. Additional support was provided by a UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center pilot grant, a Schiff Foundation grant, the Ben and Catherine Ivy Foundation, and the Focused Ultrasound Foundation.

#5702. Strengthening Healthcare Delivery Through Proactive Primary Care

Strengthening Healthcare Delivery Through Proactive Primary Care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A stroke can happen without warning. In the months beforehand, however, there may have been a blood pressure reading that needed attention, a prescription that lapsed or a follow-up visit that never got scheduled. Primary care is usually where those signals surface first, and where there is the best chance to act before an emergency.

Much of that work happens between appointments. Care teams review charts ahead of visits, call patients after a hospital discharge and follow up on overdue screenings. Traditional fee-for-service pays for the visit itself but offers little support for the proactive work around it. Value-based care shifts the focus from the volume of services delivered to the quality, outcomes and total cost of care. By aligning financial incentives with prevention, it helps keep patients healthy and out of the hospital while strengthening the long-term financial sustainability of the practice.

For people with traditional Medicare, the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) enables primary care practices to be paid for that preventive work. MSSP is a permanent, voluntary accountable care program run within traditional Medicare by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). Physician groups, health systems and community health centers participate by joining an accountable care organization (ACO), which takes responsibility for the quality and total cost of care for its assigned patients.

Clinicians continue to bill Medicare for covered services under fee-for-service, and MSSP adds a layer of value-based savings on top. When proactive primary care lowers the total cost of patients' care against a historical benchmark, often by preventing avoidable hospitalizations and emergency visits, and the ACO meets quality standards, Medicare shares a portion of those savings with the ACO. Because savings stem directly from keeping people healthy, clinical goals and financial rewards finally pull in the same direction. Shared savings are not guaranteed and depend on multiple factors.

The program operates at significant scale. In performance year 2026, 511 ACOs are serving 12.6 million people with traditional Medicare.¹ In performance year 2024, 75% of participating ACOs earned shared savings, and the program produced roughly $2.5 billion in net savings for Medicare.²

Physician-led value-based care puts primary care physicians and practices at the center of care delivery and decision-making. Shared savings give primary care organizations a revenue stream tied to prevention, which they can reinvest in staff, outreach and technology.

An ACO enablement partner can provide the data, care model support and operational infrastructure needed to identify patient needs, coordinate care and manage the ACO's reporting to Medicare, while participating primary care organizations retain control over how they deliver care. Aledade is one such partner. In fact, practices with five or more years with Aledade deliver approximately three times higher savings than the national average for non-Aledade ACOs of similar tenure.3

With that support and the actionable insights and clinical guidance it brings, primary care teams can reach the right patient at the right time, and the results show up as an emergency visit avoided, a stroke prevented or a hospital stay that never happened. For patients, prevention can mean more birthdays, more holidays and more time with the people they love.

Aledade is a physician-led value-based care company and the leading value-based care participant in MSSP.4 Aledade works alongside primary care organizations to put proactive care into practice through true financial alignment. Within its ACOs, savings are generally allocated approximately 50% to Aledade and 50% to its practice partners, with individual practice distributions weighted by quality performance and other contractual terms.⁵ That means Aledade succeeds only when its primary care partners do.

For more than a decade, Aledade has partnered with thousands of primary care organizations through the ACOs it forms and manages, providing data, technology, care model support and operational infrastructure. Together, these capabilities help clinicians identify patient needs earlier, coordinate care and build a sustainable financial model that helps direct more revenue to primary care. When primary care is financially incentivized to keep patients healthy, warning signs can be caught earlier and life-threatening events can be prevented.

1 2026 Medicare Accountable Care Organization Initiatives Participation Highlights, CMS.

2 CMS Proposes Transformational Medicare Reforms to Expand Accountable Care, CMS, July 2026.

3 Aledade analysis of CMS Public Use File of MSSP annual results through 2024; for Aledade data incorporates private CMS data for 2025; weighted average of performance for all data 2015+, incorporates Aledade 2016+ cohorts.

4 Based on internal analysis of data from the 2024 CMS ACO Public Use File.

5 Based on Aledade's standard ACO contractual terms as of January 1, 2026.

The digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was launched in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it says. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to users, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.
